Over the recent few decades, the half‐metallic ferromag- netic alloys have gained much more interest because of their unique physical properties. These materials are being extensively scrutinized due to their possible appli- cations in spintronics, magnetic tunnel junctions, mag- netic random access memories, and other spin

The half‐metallic character of new quaternary Heusler alloys CoXMnAs (X = Ru, Rh) is established along with their thermoelectric, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties. The optimization of energy suggests that alloys are stable in Y2‐type structure with a ferromagnetic character. The electronic band profile through generalized gradient approximation and modified Becke‐Johnson potential indicates the metallic character of alloys. However, with inclusion of Hubbard potential to generalized gradient approximation, the alloys depict half‐metallic character with semiconducting nature in spin‐ down state. The alloys possess high magnetic moment, CoRuMnAs has 5 μB, whereas CoRhMnAs has 6 μB, following Slater‐Pauling rule MT = ZT −24. The narrow band gap in spin‐down channel enhances the thermoelectric prop- erties. The maximum value for thermopower (|S|) obtained is 44.3 and 53.44 μV/K for CoRuMnAs and CoRhMnAs, respectively. The variation of elec- trical conductivity, Seebeck coefficient, and figure of merit affirm increasing trend with temperature, which is a good indication of materials to be used in thermoelectric technology. The mechanical stability along with ductile nature of alloys is determined through elastic constants. Further, we have calculated thermodynamic properties and have established their dependence on tempera- ture and pressure using quasi‐harmonic Debye model. The half‐metallic nature with efficient thermoelectric parameters strongly supports the possible applica- tion of alloys for spin devices and green energy generation.

dependent devices.1 These materials exhibit distinctive characteristics in the vicinity of Fermi level, depicting metallic character in one of the spin channels while insulating or semiconducting behavior in other spin direction. The band gap in one of the spin channels results in 100% spin polarization in the vicinity of Fermi level.2-7 These materials are thus suggested to produce highly spin polarized currents, which could enhance

the efficiency of magneto‐electronic devices. Members of different families of alloys, viz, Heusler, pnictides, perov- skites, chalcogenides, etc, are reported to exhibit half‐ metallic nature.8-12 Among the reported half‐metallic alloys, Heusler alloys are most attractive due to their high curie temperature (TC) and their structure similar- ity to that of zinc blend and rock salt.13,14 A large number of Heusler alloys are predicted to demonstrate half‐metallic nature, which is further confirmed by experimentalists.15,16

Based on chemical composition, Heusler alloys are grouped into three types: (a) full‐Heusler with composi- tional formula of X2YZ where X and Y are transition metals and Z is sp element. These alloys crystallize in L21‐type structure. The symmetric operations followed are either of Fm‐3m space group with prototype structure Cu2MnAl or of F‐43m space group with Hg2CuTi as a model structure. The alloy crystallizes in lateral prototype only when numbers of valence electrons of Y are larger than X. (b) half‐Heusler alloy, with C1b structure having F‐43m symmetry. These can be obtained from X2YZ type by keeping one of the X sites vacant (X = V). The compo- sitional formula then becomes XVYZ. (c) Quaternary Heusler alloys (QHAs) are derived from full‐Heusler alloys by replacing one of X atoms with different transi- tion metal atoms X′. The chemical formula of QHAs is XX′YZ. The QHA can crystallize in one of the three dif- ferent prototype structures Y1, Y2, and Y3 having differ- ence in occupancy of Wyckoff positions by X, X′, Y, and Z atoms. The prototype structure of these compounds is LiMgPdSn with the stoichiometric formula of 1:1:1:1. This group of Heusler alloys mostly crystallizes in cubic structure with F‐43m symmetry.17-20 The QHA found applications in spin‐dependent devices such as spin fil- ters, spin valves, and thermoelectric technology.21,22 Only a limited number of QHA containing both 3d and 4d par- tially filled states in the same alloy have been investi- gated. Recently, Kundu et al23 investigated such alloys by exploring two series CoX′MnSi and CoXFeSi with X′ varying from Y to Ag. CoRhMnZ (Z = Ga, Sn, Sb) alloys along with hybrid alloy Co0.5Rh1.5MnSb were synthesized and investigated through experimental techniques and theoretical methods.24 The alloys demonstrate half‐ metallic character. CoRhMnSn was found to exhibits a high TC of 620 K among the synthesized alloys. CoRhMnGe later on show TC of 760 K, which is much higher than previously reported alloys.25 Impressed by the novel features of QHA here, we investigate experi- mentally not yet synthesized CoXMnAs (X = Ru, Rh) alloys for the first time. The theme of the current study is to explore the structural and mechanical stability along with magneto‐electronic, transport and thermodynamic properties of titled alloys.

The first principle method is adopted to determine the properties of the CoXMnAs (X = Ru, Rh) alloys. The basis set chosen for present study is the linearized augmented plane wave with full‐potential formulism (FP‐LAPW) via Wien2k code.26 The unit cell space is divided into muffin tin spheres and interstitial space. The muffin tin radii for Co, Ru, Rh, Mn, and As atoms were set to 0.11, 0.12, 0.12, 0.11, and 0.10 nm, respectively. Inside the spheres, the wave function is linear combination of radial wave function times the spherical wave function, whereas for interstitial space, it has plane wave nature. The atomic like wave functions are extended up to lmax = 10, while for plane wave, cutoff parameter KmaxRMT = 7.0 is used. The generalized gradient approximation (GGA)27 is used for exchange‐correlation interaction. As GGA underesti- mates band gap for systems with d/ f electrons hence to overcome the problem, the modified Becke‐Johnson (mBJ) potential and Hubbard potential are also used for present analysis.28 The U values were checked by varying from 2.04 to 5.44 eV, and optimized values are set to Co (4.48), Ru (4.08), and Mn (4.35) for CoRuMnAs and Co (4.48), Rh (3.80), and Mn (4.35) for CoRhMnAs. An ample mesh of 4500 k points is used for Brillouin zone (BZ) integration through modified tetrahedron method. The energy and charge is said to be fully converged when the convergence criterion for energy 10−4 eV and charge 10−7 e/nm is fulfilled. For the determination of thermophysical and elastic properties, Gibbs approxima- tion and elasto‐cubic methods are employed. The trans- port properties of CoXMnAs (X = Ru, Rh) alloys are analyzed with the help of Boltzmann approximation.

The alloys CoRuMnAs (X = Ru, Rh) can be derived from Co2MnAs by replacing one of the Co atoms by 4d Ru or Rh atoms. The QHAs generally crystallze in cubic struc- ture with F‐43m space group. Depending upon which atom occupies particular Wyckoff positions, there are three nonequivalent structural configurations, referred as Y1, Y2, and Y3 types.23,29,30 The Wyckoff positions of constituents are decided by fixing the As at 4a (0, 0, 0) position, while permuting the positions of remaining atoms. The atoms occupying 4a (0, 0, 0) and 4c (0.25, 0.25, 0.25) are ordered in such a way that they form ZnS (zinc blend)‐type structure; i.e., the interaction between the atoms is strongly covalent and the atoms located at 4a and 4b (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) sites form NaCl‐type sub‐lattice, and they form strong ionic bond.14 In search of stable ground state of CoXMnAs (X = Ru, Rh) alloys,

optimization of energy was carried out in all the three configurations. The total energy of these alloys as a func- tion of unit cell volume is shown is Figure 1A,B. It has been found that for CoRuMnAs and CoRhMnAs, the most stable phase is Y2, as it has minimum energy com- pared to other two phases. The relaxed lattice constant for CoRuMnAs is 0.59 nm, whereas 0.60 nm for CoRhMnAs. The evaluated optimal values of lattice con- stant (a), ground state energy (E0), bulk modulus (B0) and its pressure derivative (B′0), and unit cell volume are reported in Table 1.

The physical properties of solids directly or indirectly depends on the electronic structure. In this context, cohe- sive energy plays an important role, which is defined as the amount of energy required to dissociate the alloy into isolated atoms. Hence, it is the measure of strength of forces or chemical bonds that bind the atoms together. Thus, it is an important parameter to determine stability of alloy.31 For QHAs, cohesive energy per atom can be calculated as ECov ¼ ECo þ EX þ EMn þ EAs 4 . Here, X rep- resents Ru or Rh. The calculated values of ECov per atom are 4.96 eV for CoRuMnAs and 4.39 eV for CoRhMnAs.
These values suggest that atoms are strongly held within alloy and thus are stable.

The electronic properties are sensitive to exchange‐ correlation potential (VXC). Therefore, approximation of VXC is challenging. The electronic band structure (BS) of the CoXMnAs (X = Ru, Rh) alloys evaluated through GGA is shown in Figure 2, where from it is apparent that alloys are metallic as there exists a dense population of energy levels at the Fermi level in both spin channels. Since GGA underestimates band gap of Mott semiconduc- tors, so to obtain the precise band profile, we have employed mBJ approximation. The band structures via mBJ method are given (Figure 3). A significant change is observed in the band structures in minority spin chan- nel across all the symmetry points of Brillioun zone with inclusion of mBJ to GGA. But the shifting of bands is not enough to produce a gap at Fermi level as the conduction band crosses the Fermi level at Γ point indicating the metallic nature of alloys. In order to have effective analy- sis of electronic profile, we have further opted GGA + U approach (where U is the Hubbard potential) to treat highly correlated states of d‐electrons. The investigated band profile is depicted in Figure 4. It is clear that states

in spin‐up channel are crossing the Fermi level, whereas in minority spin channel, neither valence band (VB) nor conduction band (CB) overlaps the Fermi level and desig- nates the half‐metallic nature of the alloys. In the minor- ity spin channel of CoRuMnAs, the top of VB and minimum of CB are at same symmetric point Γ and indi- cate the direct band gap having magnitude of 0.34 eV for CoRuMnAs, whereas CoRhMnAs has direct band gap of 0.87 eV. The contribution of individual atoms to the band formation can be elucidated by total density of states (TDOS) and partial density of states (PDOS). The atom resolved total DOS of both alloys by GGA is reported in Figure 5A,B, and by mBJ is plotted in Figure 6A,B. From the graphs, it is evident that the alloys have a metallic

character in both spin orientations. The DOS of the two alloys under GGA + U method is shown in Figure 7A, B. The s and p states have least energy and do not contrib- ute to the bands near the Fermi level for CoRuMnAs. However, As‐p state contributes to the DOS at Fermi level for CoRhMnAs. The DOS plots also confirm that alloys are conducting in majority spin channel, whereas they exhibit semiconducting character in minority spin chan- nel; i.e., they have an overall half‐metallic character. The PDOS depicts that the metallic nature in spin‐up state for CoRuMnAs is mainly attributed by the occupa- tion of Fermi level by Co‐t2g and Mn‐t2g. In CoRhMnAs, the Rh‐d states both deg, dt2g, and As‐p states with a small contribution of Co‐t2g lie at the Fermi level; Mn and As
atoms have least contribution towards occupation of Fermi level.

The total and atomic resolved magnetic moment of both alloys computed by different approximations is given in Table 2. Since GGA and mBJ methods reveal the metallic nature for CoXMnAs (X = Ru, Rh). The value of total magnetic moment obtained by GGA for CoRuMnAs is 4.92 and 5.85 μB for CoRhMnAs. The value of magnetic moment by mBJ method is 4.98 μB for CoRuMnAs and 5.97 μB for CoRhMnAs, which are close to the integral value. By using GGA + U, the integral values of the mag- netic moment are obtained 5.0 μB for CoRuMnAs and 6.0 μB for CoRhMnAs. The alloys follow MT = ZT −24 Slater‐Pauling rule were MT is total magnetic moment
Abbreviations: GGA, generalized gradient approximation; mBJ, modified Becke‐Johnson.
and ZT is the total number of valence electrons. Hence, it supports half‐metallic nature of alloys.32 It is obvious from Table 2 that Mn and Co contributes most to the
magnetic moment by all the approximations, and same can be verified from asymmetrical nature of DOS for Mn and Co atoms.

The estimation of the elasto‐mechanical nature of an alloy is remarkable in the fundamental and technical research. The understanding of the fundamental aspects of mechanical deformation and the structural properties of materials plays a crucial role in providing valuable information about the binding characteristics between adjacent planes of atoms. The structural stability and anisotropic character can be predicted based on elastic properties. The concept of elastic constants could be interrelated to the Hooke's law that states that the rela- tionship between the stress and strain is linear, when the existing stresses are small. The calculated second‐ order elastic constants along with other elastic parame- ters are reported in Table 3. For cubic crystals, the necessary criteria for existence in a stable or metastable phase are determined on the basis of mechanical stability conditions: C11‐C12 > 0, C11 > 0, C44 > 0, C11 + 2C12 > 0, and C12 < B < C11. The determined elastic constants con- vey present alloys fulfill the necessary condition, and hence, they are mechanically stable. Using the deter- mined values of elastic constants, various other elastic parameters like Young's, bulk and shear moduli, Zener Anisotropic factor, etc are determined and are also given in Table 3.
The shear and bulk moduli were determined by adopting Viogt‐Reuss‐Hill averaging scheme. The Voigt constraints of the BV and GV for the cubic system are
The condition for isotropic nature of the materials is that Zener anisotropic factors (A) should be unity.33 If

the value of A deviates from 1, then physical properties like refractive index, sound velocity, etc possess different values in different direction, i.e., anisotropic nature. For the compounds under investigation, the value of A > 1; hence, they are highly anisotropic. Because of the aniso- tropic nature of alloys, the elastic waves will travel with different velocities in different directions. We have evalu- ated the magnitude of longitudinal and transverse waves along (100), (110), and (111) directions using Bugger's relation,34 and are reported in Table 4.

The nature of interatomic forces within the alloys can be determined with the help of Poisson's ratio.35 If the value of Poisson ratio (ν) is 0.27, then the nature of alloy is ionic and for perfect covalent bonding, v must be 0.10. The calculated value of Poisson's ratio is 0.28 and 0.32 for CoRuMnAs and CoRhMnAs alloys, respectively, reveal- ing that the forces are central in nature and the alloys are ductile, since ν is more than 0.27, which confirms that the ionic bonding is dominant. The Pugh's ratio (B/G) with critical value of 1.75 is an indicator for brittle or duc- tile nature. If B/G > 1.75, then alloy is ductile, and for B/G < 1.75, it has a brittle character. The calculated value of B/G indicates that these alloys are ductile in nature. Further, the ductile nature of a material is also calculated by using Cauchy's relation CP = C12 −C44, the positive value of CP signifies ductility and negative suggests brittle nature. The calculated values confirm the ductile nature of alloys. On the basis of the calculated values of G and B, we have estimated the value of Debye temperature (θD), which measures the temperature at which the

acoustic vibrations convert into independent thermal vibrations. At lower temperatures, acoustic vibrations completely emerge from the lattice vibration. The value of θD is proportional to the average sound velocity (vm) of the material and can be determined by using the rela- tion given as follows:

Here, the various variables have their usual meanings. The value of vm can be calculated by using longitudinal (vl) and transverse (vt) velocities which themselves can be obtained from Naver's relations.
The calculated values of θD for CoRuMnAs and CoRhMnAs alloys are 487.93 and 567.23 K.

The quest for energy efficient materials especially for thermoelectric applications is a challenge for researchers and need of industrialists. Thermoelectric materials are becoming alternate sources of energy, and the applica- tions of these materials are growing rapidly. Thermoelec- tric effect is described as the recovery of waste heat into electrical energy. In this way, these materials act as power generators and coolers. The waste heat sources for such materials are industrial processes, heavy trucks, automo- biles, steel industry, and chemical processes. The mecha- nism of thermoelectric technology is based on Seebeck effect, which establishes the relation between the voltage

generated and the temperature gradient across the junc- tion (heat flux). The general expression for Seebeck coef- ficient is given by an equation, Sab ¼ dV dT, where the terms have their usual meanings.18 On the other hand, the thermoelectric coolers are based on Peltier effect, which is just reverse of Seebeck effect; thermoelectric coolers are used for cooling of electronic devices, automo- bile cooling, personnel cooling, and refrigeration.36 Ther- moelectric refrigeration is environmental friendly technology also referred as “green method” of small scale. The efficiency of a thermoelectric material is character- ized by a dimensionless figure of merit (ZT), which is

given by ZT ¼ S2σ κl þ κe , with S representing Seebeck coeffi- cient, σ defines electrical conductivity, κe and κl represent electric and lattice thermal conductivities.37 From this relation, it is clear that for achieving high figure of merit, Seebeck coefficient and electrical conductivity should be as high as possible, while thermal conductivity should be low. Since these parameters are interrelated and directly depend on carrier concentration “n,” so it is very difficult to tune these parameters independently. To derive the thermoelectric coefficients of CoXMnAs (X = Ru, Rh), semiclassical Boltzmann's equation is solved with the help of Boltztrap code under an approxi- mation of constant relaxation time (τ = 5 × 10−15) assumed to be independent of material. The basis of the approximation is that within duration of relaxation time electrical conductivity does not have sharp variation with energy on the scale of kBT.

We have calculated the Seebeck coefficient separately for spin‐up and spin‐down channels within a temperature range of 50 to 800 K for both alloys, which are presented in Figure 8A,B. Since both alloys are metallic in spin‐up state and metals normally exhibit smaller Seebeck

coefficients, the temperature variation of Seebeck coeffi- cient in spin‐up state depicts an increasing trend. The value of S at 50 K is 4.36 (6.83) μV/K for CoRuMnAs (CoRhMnAs) alloys. With the increase in temperature, the value of S enhances and becomes 41.69 (52.33) μV/K at 800 K for CoRuMnAs (CoRhMnAs). However, as the temperature reaches from 50 to 800 K, the value of S decreases in minority spin channel from 756.36 (2414.77) μV/K to 140.13 (300.41) μV/K for CoRuMnAs (CoRhMnAs). The alloys exhibit semicon- ducting nature in spin‐down channel and semiconductors usually exhibit larger Seebeck coefficient at lower temper- atures; this is due to their very low carrier concentration. With increase in temperature, carriers excite from valence bands within the gap into the conduction band.

The increase in the number of carriers results in decrease of Seebeck coefficient. The decrease of S is attributed to its inverse relation with n. The overall temperature‐ dependent behavior of thermopower can be analyzed by computing the total S using two current models under constant relaxation time approximation.38,39 The total S through the model is average S from both spin channels weighted by the corresponding conductivities and is given

by S ¼ S↑σ↑þ S↓σ↓ σ↑þ σ↓ where S↑(σ↑) and S↓(σ↓) are the values of Seebeck coefficient (electrical conductivity) in the spin‐up and spin‐down configurations, respectively.40 The graphical variation total S is presented in Figure 9. It is clear that S is positive for both alloys in whole temper- ature range indicating p‐type character of these alloys.
The maximum values of S alloy are 44.30 μV/K for CoRuMnAs and 53.44 μV/K for CoRhMnAs.

The variation of electric conductivity with temperature in spin‐up and spin‐down channels for both alloys is depicted in Figure 10A,B. Since BoltzTraP code yields (σ/τ), the dependence of τ is removed here by multiplying it with a constant value of relaxation time. From these graphs, it is evident that at 50 K, the alloys have maxi- mum conductivity of 9.75 × 105 Ω1 m−1 and 9.0 × 105 Ω−1 m−1 for Ru‐ and Rh‐based alloys respec- tively in spin‐up channel. Above 50 K, the value of σ decreases to the minimum values 7.1 × 105 Ω1 m−1 and 8.57 × 105 Ω−1 m−1 at 800 K. The value of σ in spin‐down channel at 50 K is almost 0 for both alloys. As tempera- ture increases, an enhancement in electrical conduction

is observed due to thermal excitations. The value of elec- trical conductivity reaches to maximum value of 0.19 × 105 Ω1 m−1 for CoRuMnAs and 0.49 × 105 Ω−1 m−1 for CoRhMnAs alloys at 800 K. The total σ of the half‐metallic compounds is sum of the elec- trical conductivities of both spin channels, ie, σtot = σ ↑+σ↓.40 The variation of total electrical conduc- tivity with increase in temperature is demonstrated in the Figure 11. The calculated values of σtot is 9.75 × 105 (9.0 × 105) Ω−1 m−1 at 50 K and reveal a decreasing trend for both alloys with rise in temperature. At 800 K, the values of σtot reduce to 7.29⨯105 Ω−1 m−1 for CoRuMnAs and 8.62 × 105 Ω−1 m−1 s−1 for CoRhMnAs. The elec- tronic and lattice parts contribute to the total thermal conductivity, and both vary differently with temperature.

In current study we have examined the variation of elec- tronic part only, which directly varies with carrier con- centration. Figure 12 shows a variation of total electronic thermal conductivity (κe) for both the alloys in the temperature range of 50 to 800 K. The κe shows an increasing trend. The minimum and maximum values of electronic thermal conductivity for CoRuMnAs are 0.24 W K−1 m−1 and 4.03 W K−1 m−1, and for CoRhMnAs, these values are 0.22 W K−1 m−1 and 3.93 W K−1 m−1.

The applicability of material for thermoelectric tech- nology is reflected in terms of power factor given by PF = S2σ. It also defines the efficiency of a thermoelectric material. The high power factor of a material suggests high efficiency. The variation of power factor with tem- perature is plotted in Figure 13A. The calculated value of PF increases with rise in temperature and reaches to a maximum value of 14.31 μW K−2 cm−1 for CoRuMnAs and 24.90 μW K−2 cm−1 at 800 K for CoRhMnAs. From the PF, one can directly determine figure of merit (ZT). Here, we have evaluated the ZT while considering only electronic part of thermal conductivity. The behavior of ZT with the increase in temperature is plotted in Figure 13B; the maximum value of ZT obtained is 0.28 for CoRuMnAs and 0.50 for CoRhMnAs. The increasing trend of electrical conductivity, Seebeck coefficient, and figure of merit with temperature insists that CoXMnAs alloy could be used in thermoelectric technology.

The electrical and thermal effects of any crystal depend on the atomic vibrations at equilibrium positions. The amplitude of lattice vibrations changes with rise in tem- perature and application of pressure. The investigation of thermodynamic properties provides detailed

information about performance of alloys when subjected to temperature and pressure. The overview of thermody- namic properties like, specific heat capacity, Debye tem- perature, thermal expansion coefficient, and Grüneisen parameters and their variation with pressure and temper- ature is analyzed using quasi‐harmonic Debye model.41 These parameters predict the interatomic interaction of materials. The temperature and pressure variation were chosen in the range of 0 to 975 K and 0 to 50 GPa for CoRuMnAs. Similarly, for CoRhMnAs, the range of tem- perature is from 0 to 850 K, while pressure is varied from 0 to 50 GPa. The ability of an alloy to absorb heat from surroundings and increase its temperature is expressed by its specific heat. Because of increase in temperature, the thermal vibrations in the materials increase. Thus, more input of energy is required to raise temperature of material. The alteration of Cv with temperature at various pressures for CoRuMnAs and CoRhMnAs is depicted in Figure 14A,B. It is evident that heat capacity increases with raise in temperatures. The variation of Cv increases up to 926 K for CoRuMnAs and 805 K for CoRhMnAs, respectively; beyond that, it demonstrates a constant behavior, i.e., approaches to Dulong‐Petit limit. At very lower temperatures, Cv obeys T3 law and the maximum value of Cv turns out to be 97.1 J mol−1 K−1 for CoRuMnAs and 96.4 Jmol−1 K−1 for CoRhMnAs.

Grüneisen parameter (γ) is a dimensionless quantity, which dictates the thermal state of alloys and the exis- tence of convection. It is helpful in the exploration of var- iation of anharmonicity in the crystal lattice. It is also used to analyze the change of a given mode of frequency with density. The variation of parameter with tempera- ture is presented in Figure 15A,B. From this figure, it is clear that γ increases with temperature while decreases with increasing pressure. The value of γ at T = 0 K and by varying the pressure from 0 to 50 GPa reduces from 2.097 to 1.921 for CoRuMnAs and from 1.8044 to 1.731
for CoRhMnAs. The decrease in γ because of application of pressure is due to reduction in anharmonicity, whereas with temperature, it increases.
The parameter that determines the degree of expansion under thermal energies is referred as coefficient of thermal expansion (α). This expansion mainly takes place because

of asymmetric nature of potential energy. Figure 16A,B shows the variation of “α” at different pressures and tem- perature. It is evident from this figure that α increases with increasing temperature. At lower temperatures, α increases exponentially, while at higher temperatures, it exhibits a gradual increase. This variation of α with pres- sure is opposite to that of temperature; i.e., at lower tem- perature, the effect on α is very less, but at higher temperature, the effect of pressure becomes dominant, and hence, α decreases swiftly. With increase in tempera- ture, both frequency of vibrations exhibited by constituents as well interatomic distances, whereas with applications of pressure, the vibrations are seized and atoms are brought closer. The inverse effect of temperature and pressure is due to the reason that temperature reduces the overlapping of orbitals, but pressure enhances the bonding among con- stituents. The atoms are thus held in a compact manner resulting in decrease of thermal expansion, while with rise in temperature, the strength of bonds decreases, and thus, thermal expansion increases.

Using first principle calculations, we have investigated new quaternary Heusler compounds CoRuMnAs and CoRhMnAs. The present calculations reveal that both the alloys crystallize in C1b structure with F‐43m space group and a relaxed lattice constant of 0.59 and 0.60 nm in Y2 phase. Spin‐resolved band structure affirms the half‐metallic nature of both alloys with gaps 0.34 eV for CoRuMnAs and 0.87 eV for CoRhMnAs, respectively. The alloys could be potential candidates for MRAM devices because of their high magnetic moments 5 and 6 μB and half‐metallic character. The elastic constants confirm stability in cubic structure, and Cauchy's pres- sure and Pugh's ratio suggest alloys to be ductile. Ther- moelectric properties were investigated in the temperature range of 50 to 800 K. The alteration of Seebeck coefficient and electronic conductivity signifies half‐metallic behavior of materials with holes as majority carriers. The values of Seebeck coefficient and power fac- tor reflect that the compounds may be potential candi- dates for thermoelectric applications.

The perovskite structure, ABX3 with cations occupying A and B positions, anions occupying the X‐site leads to def- inite crystalline structure. The perovskites are a loaded family of materials with countless fascinating and aston- ishing properties.1-3 Due to their application in numerous fields, perovskites with different compositions and struc- tures are intensively studied. Perovskites show various important applications as half‐metallicity, insulating nature, superconductors, semiconductors, ferroelectricity, magnetic memory, photodetectors, photocatalytic, modu- lators, lasers, etc.4-10 In the unit cell of inverse perovskite, the heavy metal atoms have exchanged positions with the nonmetal atoms placed at face centers, the nonmetal atoms at the body‐center position, and light‐metal atoms at the cube corner sites. Inverse or antiperovskites have

The state‐of‐the‐art density functional theory is used to investigate various properties of rare‐ earth based inverse perovskites Gd3AlX (X = B, N). The materials show robust structural stability at high pressures without undergoing any phase transition. The ferromagnetic character is retained at high pressures with high value magnetic moments 7.09 μB and 7.38 μB at 0 GPa for Gd3AlB and Gd3AlN, respectively. In view of Poisson's and Pugh's ratio, the ductility and brittleness of Gd3AlX (X = B, N) has been analyzed. The mechanical sta- bility is maintained throughout the pressure range with high value of Debye temperature. Transport properties have been calculated at different pressures for both the alloys, which show excellent thermoelectric properties. Besides, this the variation on some significant thermodynamic properties is also stud- ied. Our successful prediction of the stabilization of the metallic Gd3AlX (X = B, N) has proposed a route to synthesize novel rare‐earth–based inverse perovskites.

been examined since 1980 because of various interesting properties.11-13 Based on electronic structure, they can be designed as insulators, conductors, or semiconduc- tors.14,15 Inverse perovskites show decent optical proper- ties suggesting their application in the field of integrated optics.16 Cubic inverse perovskites, M3XY (M = metal; X = metalloid; Y = B, C, N, O), shows remarkable proper- ties in the fields of superconductors, giant magneto‐ resistor, metal‐insulator transistors and magnetism, nega- tive thermal expansion, magneto‐caloric effect, etc. Recently, they are emerging as potential applicants for topological insulators and three‐dimensional Dirac elec- tron systems.17 A series of rare‐earth–based inverse perovskites have been studied for various properties to find vital application in various fields.18-23 Several inverse perovskites have been prepared, characterized, and stud- ied24,25 like A3NIn, A3NSn, and A3XAl, where (A = Sc,

La, Ce, Pr, Nd, Sm, Gd‐Tm, Lu) and (X = C, N, O). The electronic and magnetism properties of Gd3AlX (X = B, N) were investigated by Kacimi et al.26 We have further extended the investigation on these materials for elastic, thermodynamic, thermoelectric, and optical properties for various applications.

The examination of pressure study plays an imperative part in understanding the thermodynamics of solids. The pressure dependence provides deeper information about various properties, which is quite helpful for understand- ing the lattice structures. Pressure tuning is also a novel approach to develop or enhance thermoelectric efficiency of the materials.27 High pressure has a robust impact on the density of states (DOS), specifically in the neighbor- hood of the Fermi level. The pressure reliance of the energy bands allows the optimization of thermoelectric properties. Therefore, it is essential to build an under- standing of how pressure influences the electronic struc- ture and hence enhances the transport properties. Therefore, investigation of materials under different pres- sure conditions is important. The present motive of the work is to study the pressure dependence of materials on various properties to observe how the material behaves under different pressure conditions.

For this study, we have used Wein2k code based on den- sity functional theory. We adopted various approxima- tions like GGA, GGA+U, SOC, and mBJ for solving the exchange correlation term.28,29 We have used Perdew‐ Burke‐Ernzerhof formulism for parametrization of XC. For strongly correlated systems, the band profile is not explained well because of self‐interaction of electrons and less potential for highly localized states. Thus, mBJ potential is applied to treat self‐interactions and various electronic states in a valuable way. For Brillouin zone

(BZ) sampling, we have used Monkhorst‐Pack scheme. A dense mesh of 3000 k‐points is used in the BZ integration. For geometrical optimization, all internal coordinates were optimized until the convergence is achieved by self‐consistent methods. The energy convergence is achieved by iterating up to 10 to 30 eV for energy and charge was less than 10‐4e. The mechanical stability of materials is confirmed by utilizing the Elastic code.30 Fur- thermore, semiclassical Boltzmann's theory under an approximation of constant relaxation time31 is used to determine the thermoelectric performance. Thermody- namics properties are calculated by Gibbs2.32
The structural, electronic, magnetic, elastic, thermoelec- tric, thermodynamic, and optical properties of Gd3AlX (X = B, N) are discussed below.

Inverse perovskite Gd3AlX (X = B, N) crystallize in cubic structure with space group Pm 3 − m at ambient pressure, as reported earlier.26 In rare‐earth–based inverse perov- skite Gd3AlX (X = B, N); Gd occupies (0.5, 0.5, 0), Al occupies (0, 0, 0); and X occupies (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) Wyckoff positions. The lattice parameter is optimized via Birch‐ Murnaghan equation of state33 in nonmagnetic and ferro- magnetic (FM) phases. They are stable in FM phase with optimized lattice constant equal to 5.04Å for Gd3AlB and 4.84Å for Gd3AlN. The optimization plots are shown in Figure 1. In addition, the cubic structure of these mate- rials is confirmed from Goldsmith tolerance factor, which is described elsewhere.34,35 The plot of total energy with unit cell volume is used to compute different parameters and is displayed in Table 1. The structure of inverse

perovskite Gd3AlX (X = B, N) is elucidated in Figure 2. To analyze the outcome of pressure on the structural properties, the bond length, unit cell volume, and lattice constant have been evaluated. The variation in lattice constant and unit cell volume with pressure is displayed in Figures 3A and 3B. It is clear that the lattice constant and cell volume decreases with the increasing pressure. The lattice constant decreases gradually with an increase in pressure by 4.365% and 3.305% in case of Gd3AlB and Gd3AlN, respectively, this is because the external pres- sure is strong enough to overcome intermolecular repul- sion in the crystal which in turn compresses the crystal.

The effect of pressure on the bond length is investi- gated for both perovskites. Figure 4 represents the bond length for all bonds of Gd3AlX (X = B, N) at different pressures. When the pressure is increased, there is a decrease in bond length but the decreasing degree of dif- ferent bond lengths is very dissimilar. When the pressure increases from 0 to 20 GPa, Gd–B, Gd–Al, and Al–X (X = B, N), bond lengths decrease consistently, as seen from Table 2. It is clear that the total decrease ratio of the Al–X (X = B, N) bond is much higher than those of any other bond lengths, showing that the Al–X (X = B, N) bond is more sensitive to compression as compared to others. Cohesive energy (Ecoh) is used to find out the strength of bonding, which is numerically equal to differ- ence of summation of energies of individual atoms and

total energy of the compound. For inverse perovskites, Ecoh can be written as Ecoh ¼ xEA atom þ yEB atom þ ZEC atom −EAxBy x þ y þ z . 36 For Gd3AlB and Gd3AlN, it is found to be 3.80 eV and 4.29 eV, respectively.

Subjugation of external loading on a crystal changes its shape as well as dimensions, which can be described by stress vector σij. Moreover, the modification in crystal structure can be determined using strain tensor εij. The generalized form of Hook's law, relating these two ten- sors, is given as σij = Cijklεkln, where the quantity Cijklεkl characterize the stiffness of material.37 The elastic con- stants are fundamentally important under different con- ditions because they provide worthy knowledge about mechanical steadiness and binding characteristics.38 The elastic constants are computed by energy‐strain relation; this is done by applying strains in small amounts to the equilibrium structure and analyzing the change in the total energy. It is important that the material satisfies sta- bility conditions at normal as well as elevated pressure; therefore, here, we checked the mechanical stability in the pressure range 0‐20 GPa. Gd3AlX (X = B, N) possess cubic structure, hence the number of independent elastic constants required is three, ie, C11, C12, and C44. The other various parameters can be derived from these inde- pendent elastic constants. Gd3AlX (X = B, N) satisfies the Born‐Huang mechanical stability criteria under applied pressure conditions.39,40 The various elastic parameters at different pressure are reported in Table 3. As pressure increases, C11, C12, and C44 increase because the inter- atomic distance gets reduced and force on bonds increases, which increases the elastic constants. We see a quasi‐linear increase of C11, C12, and C44 as a function of the pressure. Throughout the pressure range in this phase, the three axes [100], [010], and [001] are the least compressible because C11> C44 and C11> C12. Since C11> C12> C44, indicating that the shear along the [100] plane is the easiest and presents a relatively weaker resistance to the pure shear deformations, and the atomic bonds

along the [100] planes between nearest neighbors are stronger. The various parameters like Bulk (B), shear (G), and Young's (Y) moduli are used to determine the mechanical behavior of alloys. They are determined by Hill's approximation, which is average of Voigt's and Reuss's value of B and G.41 From Table 3, it is clear that Y>B>G, indicating that the materials offer maximum resistance toward deformation along the axis followed

by deformation along volumetric deformation and least resistance to shear. As pressure increases, bulk modulus also increases, indicating that these materials have high hardness and good compressibility. Furthermore, G and Y moduli increase with pressure depicting the mechani- cal stability of materials at high pressures. By considering parameters like Cauchy pressure, Pugh's ratio, and Poisson's ratio, the strength of alloys can be determined. Cauchy's pressure describes the binding character in materials, which is also related to ductile or brittle char- acteristics and is defined as Cp = C12‐C44. 42 For metallic bonding (ductile materials), the Cauchy's pressure CP is typically positive. For directional bonding (brittle mate- rials), CP is negative. The more directional bonding char- acter is characterized by large value of CP. By Pugh's ratio, one can estimate the brittle and ductile behavior of materials by considering B as the resistance to fracture and G as the resistance to plastic deformation. If B/G>1.75, then the material possesses ductile nature,

whereas B/G<1.75 is related to brittle nature of mate- rial.43 From Table 3, we see that B/G>1.75 and CP is pos- itive in the entire pressure range, indicating the ductile nature of Gd3AlB and, for Gd3AlN, B/G<1.75 and Cp is negative indicating the brittle nature in the entire pres- sure range. It is noticeable that the metallic behavior of Gd3AlX (X = B, N) increases with increasing pressure. Because of plastic deformations, brittle materials can be subjected to limited thermal shocks. The value of Poisson's ratio, “ν”, to differentiate brittle and ductile materials is 0.26. The materials with Poisson's ratio in the range 0.26<ν<0.5 are supposed to have ductile char- acter and, for 0.12<ν<0.26, the materials are supposed to be brittle.44 From “ν” value, the ductile and brittle

nature of Gd3AlB and Gd3AlN, respectively, is confirmed. Another parameter called Zener factor is defined as A ¼ 2C44 C11 −C12 , 45 which quantifies the elastic anisotropy. If “A” = 1, the material is isotropic; otherwise, material possess anisotropy. Both the materials are highly anisotropic, suggesting the low possibility of developing the microcracks or structural defects in the entire pressure range. We have calculated Debye temperature (θD) by using mean velocities as displayed in Table 4. Debye temperature is used to distinguish between low and high temperature regions for a solid given as46
θD ¼ h k 3nNA ρ 4π M 1 3vm; here, each letter has their usual meanings.

tions47 vl ¼ 3B þ 4G ð Þ 3ρ ; vt ¼ ﬃﬃﬃﬃG ρ . We have also deter- mined the phase velocities from elastic constants. Debye temperature increases from 117.12 K at 0 GPa to 193.36 K at 20 GPa for Gd3AlB and from 217.92 K at 0 GPa to 285.94 K at 20 GPa for Gd3AlN. The longitudinal and transverse modes of oscillations along particular direc- tions are calculated because the travelling waves in other directions are either quasi‐longitudinal or quasi‐

transverse in nature, as displayed in Table 5. We see that “νl” and “νt” increase with increase in pressure. The lon- gitudinal and transverse modes of oscillations along [100], [110], and [111] directions are given as

The electronic and magnetic properties of materials are important from application point of view, which can be described by considering band structure and DOS. The electronic properties of cubic inverse perovskite Gd3AlX (X = B, N) have been determined. Since we know that the electronic properties are sensitive to exchange and correlation potential, proper approximation methods should be used. Due to self‐interaction, the band gap of semiconductor or insulator is underestimated by GGA approximation. On inclusion of mBJ potential, electronic properties are expressed in a better way than other approximations, reducing inconsistency between the the- oretical and experimental results.48 Thus, to correct self‐ interaction and to treat d/f states more accurately, mBJ method is incorporated for the present analysis. The DOS plot and band structure of Gd3AlX (X = B, N) is evaluated through mBJ method for a pressure range of

0‐20 GPa. Pressure effect on electronic structure in FM configuration is shown in Figures 6 and 7. The energy bands of the alloys at ambient pressure show metallic behavior in spin up as well as spin down channels. Metal- lic character of these oxides remains as such along the applied pressure and does not show significant variation in spin up as well as spin down state in these alloys calcu- lated by different approximation methods. In order to demonstrate the electronic structure, total DOS and par- tial DOS (pDOS) were calculated in the stable phase of Gd3AlX (X = B, N) as elucidated in Figures 8–10. Almost the same, DOS is found from GGA, GGA+U, mBJ, and SOC methods. On applying the mBJ potential, the band shift fractionally close to the Fermi level in the valence band. The DOS and pDOS explain the contribution of different states in the band profile. Total DOS is calcu- lated at various pressures, which demonstrates that there is minute change in energy states for both the alloys. From Figure 11, we see that maximum contribution to DOS is due to Gd atom. As seen from the pDOS, strong overlapping of Al‐s and N‐p bands is found around Fermi level. Bottom of valence band is filled with Gd‐ f state from ‐6eV to ‐2eV, whereas N‐p and Al‐p are located between ‐5eV and ‐1eV. In valence band, there is a strong hybridization between Gd‐f , N‐p, and Al‐p states. In con- duction band, there is hybridization between Al‐p and N‐p states. From DOS, we see that there is contribution of Gd‐f states in conduction band from 3eV to 5 eV and show maximum contribution in valence band from ‐5eV to ‐4eV. The strong hybridization of Al‐p and N‐p states around Fermi level makes the compound metallic in nature. Similar is the case of Gd3AlB. The plots also divulge that the conduction band minima are pulled by the valence band which crosses the Fermi level and mak- ing them metallic.
The contributions to the magnetic moment calculated by different methods have been displayed in Table 6. The obtained magnetic moment is well consentient with

the previously reported results.26 The maximum involve- ment in the magnetic moment of the material is due to Gd element, as seen clearly from Table 6. The involve- ment of Gd to the magnetic moment can also be well understood from the DOS plot. We have calculated the magnetic properties of inverse rare‐earth–based perov- skite Gd3AlX (X = B, N) at different pressures (0, 5, 10, 15, and 20 GPa). The magnetic moments of Gd atom decrease slightly with increasing pressure, whereas the magnetic moment of B or N exhibits different behavior. The magnetic moment of Gd3AlB changes from 7.09 μB at 0 Gpa to 7.03 μB at 20 GPa. In case of Gd3AlN, it decreases from 7.38 μB at 0 GPa to 7.28 μB at 20 GPa, as displayed in Table 7. On increasing the pressure, the interatomic distance reduces, hence raising overlap of atomic states. There occurs no magnetic phase transition throughout the pressure range. The FM nature of these materials is confirmed from the susceptibility plots also. The susceptibility and their inverse plots have been plot- ted in Figure 5.

To see insight into the thermoelectric properties of Gd3AlX (X = B, N), the semiclassical Boltzmann's theory under constant relaxation time (τ = 5x10‐15s) is used. With temperature and pressure variation, thermoelectric performance of these materials has been evaluated and reported in Table 8. An efficient thermoelectric device must have small value of thermal conductivity (κ), high electrical conductivity (σ), Seebeck coefficient (S), and power factor (S2σ). The degree of these quantities enhances the thermal efficiency represented as ZT ¼ S2σT κ . 49 The thermo‐power of a material can be related to other parameters via the relation

S ¼ 8Π2k2 B 3e2 m*T Π 3n 2=3 , where kB is Boltzmann constant, m* is effective mass, and n denotes the carrier concentra- tions. Effective mass (m*) depends upon S, which is high for narrow and flat bands with large number of states per

unit of energy. At zero pressure, the increase in Seebeck coefficient with temperature is due to low charge carriers and, at high temperature, it decreases due to the increase of thermally excited electrons. In Gd3AlX (X = B, N), the conduction is mainly due to the presence of electrons, as suggested by the negative value of Seebeck coefficient. The change in Seebeck coefficient with the change in temperature at different pressure is elucidated in Figure 12. With increase in pressure, S decreases for both the materials.

The electrical conductivity (σ/τ) change with tempera- ture has been elucidated in Figure 13. We can see that σ increases with the rise in temperature. Due to the rise in amount of charge carriers, the electrical conductivity increases at high temperature. Electrical conductivity and carrier concentration (n) are related to each other as σ = neμ, where μ is the mobility and e is the electronic charge. The positive temperature dependence of electrical conductivity at high temperature is because of rise in con- centration of carriers. With the rise in pressure, the elec- tronic thermal conductivity rises for both the materials.

The thermal conductivity in solids arises due to drift of electrons and holes through the crystal, transporting heat, and phonon. The overall thermal conductivity is the sum of these two parts, ie, κ = κe+κl. The more the number of carrier concentrations, the more will be the overall ther- mal conductivity. The variation of electronic part of ther- mal conductivity with temperature is represented in Figure 14. Since BoltzTraP code evaluates only electronic part, therefore, to estimate lattice part, Slack's equation36 is used. The lattice thermal conductivity (κl) change with temperature at different pressures is reported in Figure 15 and we can see that κl reduces with the rise in tempera- ture and pressure. The total thermal conductivity (κtot) plot is described in Figure 16 and it is clear that, as tem- perature rises, κtot reduces but it raises with the rise in pressure.

The variation of power factor (PF) with temperature for Gd3AlX (X = B, N) is displayed in Figure 17. The PF has direct proportionality with temperature and inverse proportionality with pressure as it rises with the rise in temperature but reduces with the rise in pressure. The PF achieves maximum value at 800 K in both the cases. The PF is an accumulated effect of S and σ, since we know that S depends directly upon the effective mass. If we reduce the effective mass, the Seebeck coefficient gets reduced automatically, which increases the electrical con- ductivity. Thus, Seebeck coefficient plays the main part in reducing the PF.

The thermodynamic properties of the rare‐earth–based alloys have been calculated at various temperatures and pressures using the quasi‐harmonic Debye theory.50 The calculations are performed in the temperature range of 0‐430 K and pressure range of 0‐25 GPa.
The specific heat is an important thermodynamic property, which provides information about lattice dynamics and microscopic structures. The specific heat can be calculated by the equation as

harmonic approximation. This variation of Cv is plotted in Figure 18. The insets of Figure 18, for both these materials in lower temperature region Cv, shows T3 dependence, val- idating Debye's law and, with rise in temperature, it increases monotonically, validating Dulong‐Petit law. We can conclude from Figure 18 that pressure and tempera- ture have a reverse effect on specific heat because, with increase in temperature, specific heat increases, whereas, with increase in pressure, it decreases; hence, temperature has more effect on specific heat.

Apart from specific heat, another important thermody- namic parameter used to describe the thermal properties is thermal expansion coefficient (α). The temperature and pressure variation of α of Gd3AlX (X = B, N) is illustrated in Figure 19. It shows similar trend, as shown by specific heat. We observe that α rapidly increases with T3 at low pressures and gradually approach a small linear increase above 250 K for all the applied pressures. We observe that, at higher temperature and lower pressures, there is large value of thermal expansion for Gd3AlX (X = B, N).

Grüneisen parameter is the main significant thermo- dynamic parameter, which gives us information about anharmonicity in the crystal. The Grüneisen parameter is calculated and presented in Figure 20. The Grüneisen parameter remains almost unchanged with increasing temperature, but it decreases with application of pressure. The effect of temperature on Grüneisen parameter is not as significant as that of pressure. It increases very slowly at high pressure as compared to that at low pressures.

In order to determine the effect of temperature on the cubic phase, we calculated the variation of unit cell vol- ume with temperature, as shown in Figure 21, which indicates that the volumes of the materials changed slightly with temperature and no volume collapse was observed, so their phase might not change as the temper- ature increases.

The study of optical response is important for the mate- rials sustainability, robustness, and consistency in opto- electronic application.51-54 These properties can be obtained by computing the complex dielectric function ε(ω), which is written as ε(ω) = ε1(ω)+iε2(ω),

where ε1(ω) is real part and ε2(ω) is imaginary part of the dielectric function. From dielectric function, we can obtain values of refractive index n(ω), absorption coeffi- cient α(ω), reflectivity R(ω), and optical conductivity σ(ω). The various optical properties calculated are
discussed below. The pressure variation of optical absorp- tion coefficient with photon energy is shown in Figure 22. σ(ω) rises with the rise in temperature; at initial stage, the
absorption coefficient is very low and has maximum value at 7.8 eV for Gd3AlB and at 13.8eV for Gd3AlN, and it fluctuates throughout the energy range. They show

transmittance in the energy range 0‐4 eV in case of Gd3AlB and 0‐5 eV in case of Gd3AlN. They transmit UV light mainly in this region while behaving a good absorber in the energy range 8‐13 eV for Gd3AlB and

10‐13 eV for Gd3AlN. For the rest of the energy range, they behave as a reflector. Before plasma frequency, they show dielectric behavior. The optical absorption increases with increase in pressure increases; they are tunable at
high pressures for optoelectronic applications. The reflec- tivity is considered as the change in incident and the reflected power. Reflectivity specifies the surface

properties of a material. Reflectivity with photon energy is shown in Figure 23. The maximum reflectivity for Gd3AlB and Gd3AlN occurs at 0 eV and 12.5 eV at all pressures lying in the UV region of electromagnetic spec- trum. Below cut‐off frequencies, ie, plasma frequencies, there will be small reflectivity. The change in optical con- ductivity with the change in photon energy is plotted and it is concluded from Figure 24; with increasing pressure, the first peak of the optical conductivity shifts upwards in energy, whereas there is a downward shift in energy by upper peak. The larger the charge carrier concentra- tion, the larger will be the optical conductivity in the region. Gd3AlB shows maximum conductivity in the ultraviolet region corresponding to 3 eV. Other peaks are observed in the energy range 4‐5 eV, showing less conductivity in that region. With increase in pressure, σ(ω) rises and highest peak occurs at 25 GPa. In case of Gd3AlN, the optical conductivity also shows maximum conductivity in UV region and it increases as pressure increases and displays highest peak at 3 eV. Optical con- ductivity decreases up to plasma frequency and, hence,

the material stops conducting and becomes dielectric. Other important optical property we determined is refrac- tive index, which shows relation with the linear electro‐ optical coefficient, which helps us to obtain

photorefractive sensitivity of Gd3AlX (X = B, N). The change in the refractive index with photon energy is shown in Figure 25. The refractive index (R (ω)) reaches maximal values for energies near the absorption

threshold of the material. As the photon energy increases, there is no momentous variation in R(ω) with the rise in pressure. As we can see, with increase in pressure, all the optical properties increase, which is advantageous for successful employment of these material in photonic applications at high pressure.

We have successfully analyzed various properties like structural, electronic, magnetic, optical, thermal, and transport of Gadolinium based cubic inverse perovskites. The structural optimization, tolerance factor, and mechanical stability confirm Pm 3 − m cubic symmetry of both the alloys, which is in decent agreement with the earlier reported results. The pressure study confirms FM nature with no phase transition throughout elevated pres- sures. Gd3AlX (X = B, N) show high value of magnetic moment, and it increases with increase in pressure. The effect on bond length with pressure has also been studied suggesting that the total decrease in Al‐B bond is much higher as compared to others predicting its sensitiveness to compressions. All mechanical parameters increase with increase in pressure suggesting the mechanical

stability and device application at high pressure. To detect the thermoelectric efficiency, we have calculated various thermoelectric properties of these materials. Increasing nature of the thermoelectric properties with temperature and pressure convey that these materials could potentially be used for green energy generation from waste heat. Moreover, due to their good optical properties, these materials can be best used as absorbers, transmitters, and reflectors for UV light radiations for the fabrication of various optical devices.

Ferromagnetic Heusler systems being dynamic aspect for industrialists and researchers due to their advanced devel- opment in the fields like high spin polarization, remarkable electronics, thermoelectric properties, and shape-memory effect, settled in different applications such as shape mem- ory devices, spin filters and so forth.1-5 Among the half- metallic ferromagnetic (HMF) are such materials which are being predictable by the investigators deliver broader

The origin of half-metallicity, structural, thermoelectric, elasto-mechanical, and thermodynamic properties of Co2ScSb and Co2TiSb full-Heuslers has been examined by full potential methods. Structural optimizations support the sta- bility of both alloys in AlCu2Mn-prototype with space symmetry of Fm 3m (#225) space group. The occurrence of perfect band occupation and interpreta- tion of density of states through the modified version of the Becke Johnson (mBJ) scheme for both these Heusler systems delivers more precise and accu- rate results rather than GGA and GGA + U. The density of states and band occupation describes the semiconducting nature with an indirect band-gap 1.08 eV for Co2ScSb and 1.32 eV Co2TiSb. Robustness of various elastic con- stants against external forces is checked to descripted stability of these alloys. The evaluation of elastic constants and its other associated mechanical constit- uents reveals ductile behavior along with high melting temperature. The ther- moelectric coefficients are used to check the applicability of the material for waste heat recovery systems and technological purposes. Thermal parameters support the material's low anharmonicity and hence predict the stability of these alloys at the wide range of temperatures and pressure. The thermoelec- tric parameters pose its applications and stand to develop devices based on spintronics and thermoelectric purposes.

applications typically in thermoelectrics and spintronics.6,7 Thus, the spin-based electronics are predictable to convey effective developments especially in the fields like informa- tion technology (mostly in spin torque transfer and memory devices).8,9 HMF delivers 100% spin polarization presumed to promote the competence of spin-based instruments.10,11 High thermoelectric efficient materials have become an interesting area for the researchers because of providing dynamic applications typically in a waste heat recovery sys- tem.12 The efficiency for a given TE material is identified by

figure of merit (zT) indicated as zT = S2σT/κ. For a good thermoelectric efficient material, it should capable to carry high power factor (PF = S2σ) output and lower thermal durability. However, it is very hard to find such alternatives, which possess such desirable characteristics. Howsoever, the large value of ZT pronounces the best thermoelectric efficient material. Many Co2 based Heuslers like Co2FeAl,13 Co2MnAs,14 and Co2MnSi15 explored for their half-metallic, magneto-electronic and thermoelectric properties. Later on, Co2TaAl was reported experimentally to be a HMF pos- sesses lattice constant of 5.9 Å.16 Here in the present study is to expand the basic understandings of these materials for which density functional theory has been incorporated which gives an effective and precise description of computa- tional work. Hence, we expand the basic considerations, the nature of electronic structure, magnetization, elasto- mechanical properties, and their undecided thermophysical properties holding L21-structured for the first-time. The entire manuscript is allocated in different subdivisions. Section 2 is about computational insights. Section 3 eluci- dates the imperative results. Lastly, the conclusions have drawn in section 4.

To comprehend the physical properties extensively, den- sity functional simulation is significantly followed as installed in WIEN2k quantum mechanical simulation code which acts as an accurate tool to estimate ground state description of the compound. The quantity which is unknown, which needs to be estimated, is the potential due to exchange-correlation (VXC) interactions. So, (GGA)17 along with (GGA + U) with onsite coulomb interaction (U)18 have to be selected by substituting U by Ueff. Here, Ueff = U−J where J is the onsite exchange interaction and U is the onset coulomb term after being optimized to deliver more precise band profiles for pre- sent set of alloys. In Co2XSb, Co possesses seven valence electrons in the d-orbital and Coulomb potential (Ueff) was varied by adjusting J = 0−0.4. The optimized Ueff for Co was initiated to be 0.44 Ry (5.98 eV). As GGA and GGA + U formulism are somehow in adequate to explain the magneto-electronic structure of correlated systems accurately. Therefore, modified Becke Johnson (mBJ)19 has been utilized to figure out the exchange correlation which mainly assembled of d and f-states. The mBJ potential is illustrated as VmBJ x,σ rð Þ = CVBJ x,σ rð Þ + 3C−2 ð Þ 1Q ﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃ 5=12 p ﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃ 2tσ rð Þ=ρσ rð Þ q where, tσ rð Þ = 1 2 PNσ i rψ* i,σ: rψi,σ repre- sents kinetic energy with ρσ rð Þ = PNσ i ψ* i,σ:ψi,σ a charge density. The valence and core states are separated with a value of 7.0 Ry. The muffin-tin radii (RMT) are set to

prevent electron charge leakage within the interstitial sites. The wave function inside sphere is extended up to lmax = 12 and RMTKmak = 7 was set for the present alloys. An ample mesh of 4500 k-points is used for Brillouin zone (BZ) integration via; tetrahedron scheme. Thermo- dynamic investigation of various potentials is checked by Gibbs2 package.

A structural property defines a crucial role in understanding the occupation of atoms in their respective positions. The placement of atoms in their unit cell structure of Co2XSb (X = Sc and Ti) is shown in Figure 1. In Co2XSb, Co atoms occupy two equivalent positions (1/4, 1/4, 1/4), Co-II (3/4, 3/4, 3/4) within the unit cell, X = Sc and Ti shows its occu- pancy at (0, 0, 0) and Sb sites at (1/2, 1/2, 1/2). To deliver the comment on the structural stability of these alloys we correctly evaluation the ground state properties expending the Murnaghan's equation given as;

With E0, V0, B0, and B00 representing the minimum thermodynamic energy, volume, bulk modulus, and its pressure derivative B0, respectively. The unit cell struc- tural optimization is carried out in Non- magnetic (NM) (N"=N#) and Ferromagnetic (FM) (N"=N") proto- type Cu2MnAl20 configurations to display its stability and minimum energy. The alloys Co2XSb (X = Sc and Ti) are initiate to demonstrate minimum energy in Fm 3m sym- metry with ferromagnetic character as is illustrated via optimized stability curves displayed in Figure 2. The vari- ous physical properties of Co2XSb (X = Sc and Ti) are fetched and are collected in Table 1. The estimation of cohesive energy supports the stability of the present alloy and suggests that atoms in their corresponding lattice positions are strongly held together and preserves its structure over a wide range of forces. Remarkably, the formation energy of these materials signifies that they can be predicted experimentally.

The electronic structure study of a material is extremely desirable for the application based perspective. For spintronic device application the efficiency of a material is typically signified by the energy band-gaps. In this pre- sent report, we have calculated the band structure of these alloys for which we have implemented the different

approximation functional to describe the electronic behavior. The calculation of band structures was signifi- cantly done by employing all the three approximation including GGA, sophisticated GGA + U correction and mBJ which reproduces the energy band gap close to the experimental results are presented in Figure 3. The obser- vation of band gap through GGA approach in up as well as spin-down channel designates the character of metallic nature for Co2TiSb alloy, while a semiconducting gap is followed of 0.46 eV for Co2ScSb alloy in spin down chan- nel. In other words, we can say it fails to give the perfect nature of energy band gap in these materials. Henceforth, GGA + U correlation scheme is used to eliminate this ambiguity. The present U value was accurately adjusted with a U value equals to 0.44 Ry (5.98 eV) for Co-d orbital electrons. But the calculation through the Hubbard cor- rection which mainly comprises such correlated electrons is somehow inadequate to do the functionality of these Heusler systems, so mBJ potential was concerned which designate the best promptness of the theoretical results concerning their precise band-gap nature in these Heusler systems. The main advantage of this inbuilt potential is due to its exact analysis for the investigation of energy band gaps in these alloys.

Looking toward GGA correlation scheme the up-spin channel as indicated by an arrow is metallic in nature while a small forbidden semiconducting gap is seen in down-spin channel. For Co2ScSb conduction band max- ima (CBM) is at X = 0.23 eV and valence band maxima (VBM) is positioned at Γ = −0.24 presents an indirect band-gap, while Co2TiSb is metallic in both spin chan- nels. For GGA + U, the CBM located at X = 0.24 eV in up-spin and VBM at Γ = −0.28 eV in down spin brings an indirect band-gap of 0.52 eV for Co2ScSb alloy. Also, the CBM for Co2TiSb is fixed at X = 0.02 eV and VBM at

Γ = −0.41 eV offers an indirect band-gap of 0.43 eV. How- ever, in mBJ scheme, the up-spin is conducting while as spin-down proposes a gap of 1.08 eV for Co2ScSb and 1.32 eV for Co2TiSb. For mBJ, the VBM for Co2ScSb placed at Γ = −0.29 eV and Co2TiSb is at −0.85 eV; while the bot- tom of the conduction is in between Γ and X = 0.79 eV for Co2ScSb and X = 0.47 eV for Co2TiSb in down spin. Hence, Co2XSb (X = Sc, Ti) obviously have minimum gap of energy in down spin channel while undertaken with both GGA and GGA + U approximations which is also observer from the DOS plots shown in Figure 4. However, advanced mBJ functional generates the large half-metallic gap. The inter- pretation of band structures in above said schemes in terms are density of states. The presence of energy bands mainly from conduction region in spin minority state of Co2TiSb shows occupancy of bands close to the Fermi level, which suggests the peculiarity of band character is n-type and hence the carrier capability of heat transport is obviously due to the electrons which acts as dominant carriers for such kind of alloy. However, In Co2ScSb reverse case is observed which concludes p-type charge carries as suppliers. In nutshell, we predicted that the current conduction within Co2TiSb is due to the presence of electrons, rather than holes in Co2ScSb which are responsible to carry the electri- cal conduction processes in such type of Heusler systems.

Next, we have tried to understand the elemental contri- bution and visibility of atomic states in these alloys which were thoroughly investigated by the (mBJ) functional scheme, hence partial densities of states (pDOS) are plotted as shown in Figure 5. The activeness of d-states of Cobalt and Titanium atoms are more populated due to the fact of pres- ence of d-states which leads a sufficient quantity of magne- tism toward the cell structure. The Antimony p-states are low lying deep states carrying little visibility hence the contri- bution toward magnetic structure in these alloys is low. How- ever, from the graphical plots of pDOS it is completely visible that the Fermi level is mainly assembled by these d-states in both the alloys and reflects that strong d-d hybridization is preserved within such kind of L21 structured alloys. How- ever, the band channels and also its interpretation in terms of its associated DOS designate the robust half-metallic char- acter due to which the 100% spin polarization effect is predicted in such kind of alloys. Hence, the capability of
containing an essential tunable band-gap poses a supportive stand in high performance electronic devices to meet the requirements of present technological demands.

Also, the report carries an essential outstanding prop- erty regarding these alloys is magnetism. The description of these alloys in terms of magnetic properties as justified as potential application feature in spintronic technology and other spin based fields. The present calculation takes the full potential use of GGA, unified GGA + U, and mBJ schemes to obtain the magnetic moment in case of these alloys as shown Table 2. From the table the Co atom in different approximations plays a demonstrating role to carry out sufficient magnetism in corresponding magnetic structures. However, the impact of magnetic moment of remaining atoms also contributes to the cell structure, which accounts the total magnetism in both the alloys. The recorded value of magnetism found in Co2ScSb and Co2TiSb is a numerical integral value equals to 2.00 μB, which is therefore the characteristic feature of ferromagnetic materials. In other words the materials are both ferromagnetic in character in accordance with the positive magnetic moment present in such Heusler sys- tems. It is obvious to see that the atoms having the + sign convention descripts the parallel alignment of spin with respect to the neighboring atoms and negative mark indi- cates the ferri or antiferromagnetic spin arrangements. Hence, the net magnetism due to these atoms gets reduced. Henceforth, from the magnetic study of these beneficent alloys it can be seen that these materials could be predicted to be the promising candidates for mul- tiferroic and magnetoresistive for spintronics and high performance electronic devices applications.

The elastic properties decide the mechanical stability of the material. Hence, the materials linked with better elastic properties projects their high stand in techno- logical and industrial based perspective needs. The elastic constants reproduce the other mechanical parameters to determine the materials capability under various external forces. In this report we have make an

attempt to calculate the elastic properties of Co2ScSb and Co2TiSb Heusler alloys. With the estimation of Birch Murnaghan's second order derivative, since the characterization of these materials displays in cubic structures, so C11, C12, and C44 are required to eluci- date other mechanical properties. To describe the structural stability, the suitable stability criterions

conditions can be mathematically conveyed as C11 + 2C12 > 0; C11 −C12 > 0; C11 > 0 and C44 > 0. is followed.22 Both Co2ScSb and Co2TiSb materials satisfy the stability criteria, indicating that both materials with cubic conformation are mechanically stable.
Elastic anisotropy (A) outlines a crucial role in defin- ing the micro-cracks at growing process.23 If A = 1, then

the crystal is prescribed to be completely isotropic, if the values lies below the unity signifies elastic anisotropy. Hence, the calculated results observed from the Table 3 depict that both Co2ScSb and Co2TiSb Heuslers are highly anisotropy. To classify the plastic performance of material, Pugh's ratio (B/G) has the limit value 1.75.24 If B/G > 1.75, the material is ductile otherwise brittle nature is conveyed. Since B/G ratio for both alloys are greater than critical value indicates that these materials possess ductile nature. Hence, poses its fruitful applica- tions in tensile compression. Also, another stability crite- rion followed by the materials is Frantsevich's ratio (G/B)25 having their corresponding numerical value which are less than 1.06, designates that these alloys are possessed shear deformation against low resistance.

The Poisson's ratio (ν) is another factor used to separate the materials via ductile or brittle.26 (ν) also designates the nature and bonding forces preserved in the material. If its value is >0.26 the material retains ductile nature otherwise the material acts as a brittle. (ν) also delivers the evidence about the bonding forces existing in the materials. For cen- tral force in the solids, the Poisson's ratio has a boundary of 0.25 to 0.5. From our calculated values the (ν) lies in this range, suggests that the bonding forces are of central type for these alloys. Cauchy's pressure (CP) provides direct information whether the material is brittle/ductility.27
Since, the value of (CP) for Co2ScSb and Co2TiSb is found to be equal 2.05 and 30.41, respectively, which also predicts that these alloys are ductile in nature.

The Kleinman parameter (ξ)28 computes internal strain and thus designates the comparative ease of bond bending against bond elongating. In a structure, reduc- ing bond bending indicates to ξ = 0 and diminishing bond stretching indicates to ξ = 1. For Co2XSb the ξ parameter is 0.59 for Co2ScSb and 0.58 for Co2TiSb. Hence, Co2TiSb reflects slightly more resistance to bond bending in comparison to Co2ScSb. Hence, the clarifica- tion of elastic constants and its associated mechanical parameters demonstrates its strength against numerous external forces, which there by offers a potential stand in industrial based purposes.

Recurrent use of global energy crises and environmental pollution has undoubtedly laid an intensified research interest for the creation of clean energies and new elec- trochemical storage energy.1-6 The actinide-based mate- rials possesses an extending application stand in radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) where the

For the first time, we computationally investigated the alloys Ba2MgMO6 (M = U, Np) to understand the electronic structure, mechanical stability, mag- netic character, and thermoelectric along with the thermal behaviour of actinide perovskite-type oxides by high-throughput tactics. The chemical com- position of polar covalent bonding is visualized from charge density plots. The employment of mix of two parametrizations Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof generalized gradient approximation (PBE-GGA) and sophisticated Hubbard correction (GGA + U) while defining electronic structure claims Ba2MgMO6 (M = U, Np) a semiconducting material. The occurrence of minimum energy is achieved by minimizing Brich Murnaghan's equation of state in different phases, which supports non-magnetic and ferromagnetic behaviours, respec- tively, which also gets confirmed from their total spin magnetic moments. Strength among various polycrystalline mechanical constants features the duc- tile and incompressible capability, which leads to promising route towards industrial perspective needs. The analysed value for Seebeck coefficient turns out to be 291.86 and 197.08 μVK−1, respectively, for both the ordered alloys. The pressure and temperature effect on thermodynamic quantities has been keenly explored from Gibbs 2 code to figure out the stability. Hence, the over- all description of these alloys may lend its extending stand in semiconductor devices and radioisotope thermoelectric generator applications.
