The advan- tages of these perovskites are found to be astonishing with its efficiency rising above 20% and efficient in absorbing light. The perovskites have been further updated into new class of materials called double

perovskites (DPs) recognized by ordered formula A2BB0O6.9 Having their spectacular performance along with intriguing multidimensional novel application towards thermoelectric technology, they are the striking novel applicants due to their environment-friendly, non- toxic nature, lower processing cost compared with con- ventional chalcogenides, better oxidation resistance, and high-temperature stability.10-12 With such spell-bound applications, their electronic structures are frequently ranging from insulating to metallic and even half metallic along with spin-polarized electrical conductivity13,14 and superconductivity.15 As a result, they are of great techno- logical importance, with a sufficient possibility in dielec- trics or piezoelectric, electronic devices, and sensors,1 magnetic memory,3 electrolyte materials for fuel cells,16 and components for solar cells.17 Besides these numerous advancements, they are the special cases of showing tunnelling magnetoresistance and curie temperature well sufficient at room temperature.3 DPs have revolutionized the scientific community and are in demand as the mag- netism in these perovskites is considered. These layered alloys display a significant quantity of magnetism due to the fact of two magnetic sites especially B and B0, which probably contribute the aid of magnetism in such kind of systems. The magnetic behaviour can be understood from the oxide perovskites including Ba2FeMnO6 18 and Ba2MTaO6 (M = Mn, Cr).19 Simple cubic perovskites especially BaCfO3 20 and BaBkO3 21 possess an essential quantity of magnetism in their corresponding lattice structures and also designate the half metallicity for which spin-polarization effect is commonly seen in these materials. Currently, a lot of research is going on theoret- ically as well as experimentally to expand the properties of these fascinating alloys as having their surplus impact on modern era. Back in 1961, ferromagnetic double pervoskites were reported by Longo and Ward.22 Since then, they have been explored for their outstanding prop- erties. However, the discovery of half metallicity as well as semiconducting behaviour preserved in such alloys has paved a keen attention towards these double perov- skite materials. Mg-based perovskites are best suited for promising anode materials.23 Analogous to halide type, complex perovskites have lured the scientific community due to the advancement of photovoltaic research and its potential to overcome the instability and toxicity issues of Pb-based hybrid perovskites.24 It is expected that studying of high number of possible combination with change of B0 and B00 in A2B0B00X6 can provide the opportunities of finding effective alternatives.25 However, the characteri- zation of Ba2MgUO6 was experimentally studied and was prepared by Sleight and Ward.26 Further studies were carried by Sack and Seemann.27 Both Ba2MgMO6 (M = U, Np) complex perovskites adopt the cubic

geometry along with space symmetry Fm-3m. Hence, in the present set of calculations, we are using the basic information regarding from their lattice parameters to predict the essential properties for which density func- tional theory (DFT) has systematically recommended to simulate the basic understanding in these materials.

Despite being synthesized experimentally, the main aim to carry this piece of work is to find its place in energy harvesting technologies, for example, thermoelectric and power resources. So, for the exploration of these materials to be considered, an extended version of DFT is strictly followed, which enhances the properties of solid materials prior to the experimental results, based upon band theory calculations integrated in WIEN2K quantum simulation package.28 The Kohn Sham equation is written as follows:

The first term on RHS side arises due to electron- nuclei interaction, the second term serves as electron- electron interaction (Hartree potential), and the third term exhibits potential due to exchange correlation. The exchange correlation (Exc) needs to be determined as the physical properties get deteriorated. So the first imple- mentation is achieved via PBE-GGA functional as suggested by Perdew et al.29 In such formulism, the exchange correlation (Exc) is assumed as a functional of local density and its gradient. However, PBE-GGA is inadequate due to its inconsistency in the self-interaction between the electrons. The underestimation of PBE-GGA over exchange correlation is one of the widely discussed anomalies in electronic structure predictions. Therefore, the exact density of states (DOS) due to self-interaction error and insufficient potential for highly energy states needs to be addressed by the application of more sophisticated Hubbard correction parameter (GGA + U).30

The inclusion of Hubbard model in a meaning full way Ueff (Ueff = U −J) where the (U) term stands for Cou- lomb repulsion was taken 0.35 Ry, and exchange interac- tion (J) was slightly altered from 0 to 0.04 eV for both U and Np f-orbitals. For the present set of calculations, the contributions to the potential are accounted from core as well as valence states. Matrix geometry in the basis set is chosen and is determined by product of RMT kmax = 7 where RMT describes smallest muffin-tin radii, which are set to prevent electron hopping from core to interstitial regions, and kmax stands for the plane wave expansion. The selected energy separation of value −7.0 Ry between the inner core and valence states favours the better energy convergence. A mesh of 10 × 10 × 10 points is uti- lized, which certifies the convergence of 1000 k points together with total energy 10−4 eV and energy 10−4 Ry for accurate self-consistent calculations.

Structural properties reveal a crucial role in predicting the atomic occupancy at different lattice sites and also picture the bonding in between them. In this study, the materials display their structural arrangement of atoms in face-centred cubic Fm-3m symmetry. The Ba2MgMO6 (M = U, Np) consists of two sublattices crystalizes in a geometry in which four distinct elements in the ratio of 2:1:1:6 forming the DP unit cell structure mentioned in Figure 1. The unit cell of DP is twice the size of simple cubic perovskite cell. The position of larger cation Ba with 12-fold coordination resides at body centre having Wycoff 8c: (0.25,0.25,0.25), Mg and U/Np, which are responsible for the shape formation, are located at 4b: (0,0,0), 4a: (0.5,0.5,0.5) within the centre of O anion placed at 4e: (х,0,0), x = 0.25 at crystallographic corner sites forming alternate MgO6 and U/NpO6 octahedrons, respectively. Therefore, the resulting materials with better mechanical parameters challenge their high stand in technological- and industrial- based requirements. The computed values of both the oxides estimate that Young's modulus is comparatively large and shows prom- ising feature in engineering and technological applica- tions. Voigt-Reuss-Hill (VRH) approximation38 is an approximation of calculating bulk and shear modulus. The values of bulk modulus indicate the maximum resis- tance offered by these alloys towards the volumetric change caused by external pressure. Furthermore, Pugh's ratio (B/G)39 correlates the material to be brittle or duc- tile. Its index value is 1.75, that is, if B/G is exceeding than 1.75, ductility of the material is conveyed otherwise as brittle nature. From Table 3, it is seen that the value of B/G of these compounds is greater than its critical value that supports ductile feature and thus shows their inter- esting properties related to bending, tensile, and com- pression. Another mechanical stability criterion called

Poisson's ratio (ν) also illustrates that the stability condi- tion and its value more than 0.26 portray the ductile character. Poisson's ratio also divulges the ductile charac- ter of these materials. In a similar manner, Cauchy's pressure denoted as C00 = (C12-C44)40 also clarifies the possession of ductile ability of these layered alloys. Posi- tive value hints that the material is ductile, and negative corresponds to brittle. In this study, Cauchy's pressure for both the materials is positive and hence supports the ductile nature of these present oxide materials. From the data values reported in Table 3, it is shown that both the materials are anisotropic and cubic in nature. Therefore, the elastic waves propagating in these crystal structures are directionally dependent. The pure modes of longitudinal as well as transverse veloci- ties can only exist in three different directions ([100], [110], and [111]) and can be calculated through Brugger's relation. The longitudinal (vl), transverse (vt), and average (vm) velocities are approximated and are collected and quoted in Table 4.

The observed values of melting temperature for both the alloys are 1806.36 and 1807.90 K, respectively, and therefore propose the capability of these materials to retain their ground-state structures over a wide range of temperatures.

The band structure of a material elucidates an essential description about the electrical properties of material. In this report, we have calculated zero pressure and temper- ature band structures along high symmetric directions of Brillouin zone (BZ) of Ba2MgMO6 (M = U, Np) perov- skite systems based upon spin-polarized DFT within GGA and GGA + U functional schemes. Since PBE-GGA is unable to predict the exact band structure of the mate- rials. Therefore, the more sophisticated GGA + U approximation was employed which provides empirically an exact precession, close to the experimental results by varing the potential to correct exact band structure. Hence, Hubbard potential has conveniently been employed in these calculations to provide an essential physical description on these alloys regarding its band structure as well as for DOS. The calculated spin- dependent band profiles along with the total DOS (TDOS) in PBE-GGA and GGA + U functional schemes present the semiconducting nature of these layered alloys in both the spin channels as shown in Figure 3A-H. From the illustration of bands because of its symmetric nature, the complex alloy Ba2MgUO6 in GGA and GGA + U approximation demonstrates that the conduction band lowest energy level and valence band highest energy are located at 1.98/2.68 and 0.01/0.03 eV along the same K symmetry point with a band gap of 2.00 and 2.71 eV, respectively. Similarly, for the case of Ba2MgNpO6 towards its spin-up displays, the corresponding conduction band

minima and valence band level maxima levels are sub- stantially at 1.17/2.69 and 0.004/0.001 eV, and for spin down, the values are at 1.49/3.28 and −1.06/−0.01 eV, leading to the tunable band gap of 1.17 and 2.69 and 2.55 and 3.30 eV, respectively. Thus, GGA and GGA + U methods reveal that both the actinide materials are semiconductor-type perovskites. However, in semicon- ductor materials, energy gap increases with respect to temperature due to which the lattice vibrations increase, which in turn increase larger interatomic spacing. The interaction between the lattice phonons, free electrons, and holes will also affect the band gap to a smaller extent.45 Varshni's empirical approximation46 is used to find the relationship between band gap energy and tem- perature and is expressed as
where Eg(0), α, and β are linked with the material constants.

In a well-arranged crystal semiconductor, the corresponding energy gap is somehow fixed, which there- fore shows the continuous energy states but for the case of quantum dot is size dependent and can be altered by somehow band gap engineering techniques. This is related to quantum confinement effect. Hence, the overall sce- nario of band structure and also its associated TDOS as portrayed in Figure 4A,B reflects its semiconducting nature. On examining from E-k curves in all the band pro- files, it is evident that conduction band bottom is less dis- persive having almost flat bands along all the highly symmetric points. Therefore, the carriers either electrons or holes responsible for the electrical conductivity can pos- sess high effective mass, which in turn leads to increase in power factor also. Further, the inspection of understand- ing the elemental contribution (pDOS) for both the layered alloys through the approximation scheme of GGA + U as shown in Figure 4C-F shows the presence of energy states that touches tangentially from the valence band to the Fermi level in both the spin directions, which are the Mg- p, U-p, and O-p in Ba2MgUO6. Similarly, for Ba2MgNpO6, Mg-p, Np-p along with the O-p are the states which are responsible to show visibility near to the Fermi level. How- ever, these states from the conduction region in spin- minority channel depict a little bit shifting movement from the Fermi level presenting a forbidden gap between valence band and conduction band. Thus, presenting semiconducting behaviour in both of these alloys is pre- served within their lattice structures. Recently, DFT study on experimentally determined, uranium-based DP Ba2NiUO6 31 also supports that the semiconducting nature is preserved within such type of alloys.

Next, we have made an effort to find the origin of mag- netic moment and charge density (CD). So, first, observ- ing its magnetic study as magnetic properties is directly linked to the structure of the materials, particularly its

electronic configuration. Magnetic moment regarded as a fundamental property decides the magnetic strength of a material. In the light of the present study, we are engaged with different correlation schemes including GGA and GGA + U to figure out the magnetism in these alloys. From Table 5, it is clearly seen that the magnetic moment associated with Ba2MgNpO6 is 1μB, which is

due to the involvement of Np atom having their one- half–filled electron spin in 6d orbital corresponds to its magnetization. On the other hand, from the DOS as well as band structure, it triggers its prominent spin polariza- tion at the Fermi level. The low-lying bands that are far away from the Fermi level usually corresponds to s bands, which projects least magnetism. The positive value of magnetic moment indicates parallel spin

alignment corresponding to the other constituents. Henceforth, the capability of containing magnetic moment clearly poses its stand for spintronic and mem- ory shape devices. Since, the material Ba2MgUO6 is non- magnetic in character, which also gets clarified from their dos plots as well as symmetric band structures within the two approximation schemes; hence, no quan- tity of magnetism is estimated in such an alloy.

Further understanding graphically the electronic CD as displayed in Figure 5 also provides complete and con- cise study about the nature of hybridization among the various atomic orbitals. Here, we have examined the CD plots in (110) plane to envisage the chemical bonding. Therefore, this study comprises the covalent character between oxygen and uranium while linkage between bar- ium and magnesium is ionic in nature. Similar kind of bonding is also detected in Ba2MgNpO6. Henceforth, the overall study confirms that the polar covalent bonding that is, add mixture of covalent and ionic, is well kept in these semiconductor alloy systems.

Thermoelectric phenomena carried by the materials pro- vide an essential clue and fascinating prospect of conver- ting squander heat (thermal energy) into usable electrical power energy. Because of subsequent dramatically envi- ronmental changes, energy resources get vanishing or depleting, which poses an exerting threat for sustainable life. This enforces to look on new materials to remove such kind of problems. The scientific body is busy in find- ing the specific alternatives (sources), which are eco- friendly, cost-effective, and highly efficient.10-12 Late

back, it was predicted that quantum confinement for the charge carriers is responsible to enhance the thermoelec- tric efficiency. In such situations, half Huesler alloys alongside with skutterudites, clathrates, and silicides were used in practice to tackle the problems. The short- comings of poor durability at high temperatures and low

abundance found in such materials are incapable in wide commercialization purposes. Thermoelectric oxide mate- rials in this regard are considered to encounter these dif- ficulties, which are prominent incompetence sources. To ensure large the- rmopower, the carriers should be of only one type, either p-type or n-type as a mixed type of carriers cancels each other's effect, reducing the generated potential. The thermopower of a material can be characterized by the following equation:

Here, S is directly proportional to effective mass (m*), which is seen high for narrow and flat bands, tracking down towards the thermoelectric response of Ba2MgUO6 and Ba2MgNpO6 oxides in the neighbourhood of Fermi level. Here, we have made an easy attempt to forecast thermoelectric response of these materials with the advantage of Boltzmann's theory under constant relaxa- tion time and rigid band approximation.54,55 The theory is integrated in the BoltzTrap code and is quite useful for understanding various transport coefficients inclusive of Seebeck (S), electrical conductivity (σ/τ), thermal con- ductivity (κ), and associated power factor (PF). These transport coefficients have been rigorously studied to descript the character of converting amount of waste energy into useful form. Thus, the results offered here are based on Boltzmann's transport theory. In order to comment on Seebeck coefficient or thermopower portrayed in Figure 6A outlines the creation of voltage in response to temperature gradient labels decrease in its value. The decrease of Seebeck for the two oxides Ba2MgUO6 begins from higher value 848.46 μVK−1 at lower temperature of 50 K to 176.2 μVK−1 at 800 K, and for Ba2MgNpO6, it exponentially decreases from 228.13 to 150.62 μVK−1 along the above-said temperatures. This decreasing nature of Seebeck (S) especially in semicon- ducting materials is due to increase in the carrier concen- tration and thereby offers more electron hole pairs, which in turns leads to more scattering effects that turns Seebeck to decrease. Next, the electrical conductivity (σ/τ) displayed in Figure 6B over the relaxation time con- stant (τ = 5.1 × 10−15 s) increases. The reason is that

semiconductor materials have negative temperature coef- ficient; that is, their resistance decreases as the tempera- ture linearly increases. The case study for Ba2MgUO6 and (Ba2MgNpO6) over electrical conductivity increases with

the increasing low-temperature value of 50 K, which is almost 0 and 0.09 to 1.07 Ω−1 m−1 s−1 (1.51 Ω−1 m−1 s−1), respectively. It is noticeable that pseudo gaps present on either sides at the Fermi level affect its decrease in
electrical conductivity, in order to have insight on lattice thermal conductivity,56,57 which particularly governs the contribution of phonons in these semiconductor systems
that mainly act as heat transporters in materials. The heat energy of these materials is transported by two mechanisms: first, the drift of electrons, and second, by

holes through the crystal contributing the electronic part (κe) and travelling of phonons giving rise to lattice part (κl), which is (κ = κe + κl). The main pitfall of the BoltzTrap code is that although it extracts the results for electronic part (κe), the lattice part (κl) is completely unknown. So, for that reason, we have computed the lattice thermal conductivity with the help of Slack's equa- tion to determine the phonon contribution elucidated as follows:
where the letters in above expression descript usual meanings. The constant A is summarized as

The estimated value of thermal conductivity for both representative perovskites is shown in Figure 6C,D where the contribution of electronic (κe) towards thermal con- ductivity begins from 0 W/mK at 50 K to 1.07 W/mK at 800 K. On the other hand, in Ba2MgNpO6, (κe) shows a similar increasing variation from 1.69 to 1.99 W/mK. The increasing trend of (κe) also evidences the semiconducting character in such systems. In addition, the lattice part, which composes of lattice vibrations (phonons), shows a remarkable exponential decrease against temperature of 50 K with a value of 9.55 to 0.53 W/mK for Ba2MgUO6. Similarly, in Ba2MgNpO6, lattice thermal conductivity decreases from higher value of 9.14 to 0.49 W/mK. In fact, lattice thermal conductivity of Ba2MgNpO6 in comparison with Ba2MgUO6 is slightly low due to higher value of Debye temperature as lattice thermal conductivity is inversely related to Debye temperature. The scattering effect and low group velocity of phonons may be responsi- ble for decrease in its value. Power factor, an another determination closely related to DOS, demonstrates per- fectly thermoelectric performance of material depicted in Figure 6E. It is claimed that materials with high power factor generate more energy, in order to comment on the performance of these complex perovskite alloys Ba2 (MgUO6, MgNpO6) by using the DFT techniques. The power factor rises with a linear rise in temperature, which shows a logarithmic growth from a minute value almost 0 to 3.32 W/msK2 at higher temperatures for Ba2MgUO6. Similar trend is followed by Ba2MgNpO6 with a power fac- tor value of 0.51 to 3.42 W/msK2. The large value of power factor and decaying value of lattice thermal conductivity characterize these alloys to have potential stand in ther- moelectric applications.

Thermodynamic properties are required to configure the materials carrier capability, and it also relates the cause and effect of dynamics and microstructure of the mate- rial. The investigation of the thermal effects in this pre- sent study is in accordance within the quasi-harmonic Debye theory shown in Figure 7A-F without having much complicated lattice dynamic calculations where in this framework, non-equilibrium function is described as follows58,59:

Specific heat (Cv) is an authenticative aspect regard- ing the specific performance of solids under the circum- stances of pressure and temperature. Here, the specific energy performance of the materials Ba2MgUO6 and Ba2MgNpO6 has been analysed in the pressure range of 0 to 35 GPa and temperature ranging from 0 to 800 K for both the alloys. The Cv along with the temperature of both the alloys increases rapidly up to 400 K, as the tem- perature increases, which causes the increase in specific heat, thereby offer a material to follow well-known Dulong Petit's law. The predicted values of specific heat of Ba2MgUO6 and Ba2MgNpO6 alloys at 300 K are 201 and 203 J/mol/K, respectively.

Grüneisen parameter (γ) is one of the essential thermo- dynamic parameter insights the quantitative understand- ing of macroscopic behaviour of solids in physics. It is also considered an important dynamical property used to quan- tify the relationship between thermal and elastic descrip- tion of solids and is directly connected with them. Here, for the case of Ba2MgUO6 and Ba2MgNpO6, the Grüneisen parameter (γ) shows an increasing inclining trend with increase in temperature but on the other hand shows radi- cal decrease with increase in pressure. The calculated values scrutinized for both layered alloys Ba2MgUO6 and Ba2MgNpO6 at 300 K are 2.05 and 2.10, respectively.
Thermal coefficient (α) of a material is a tendency to change the dimensions on the application of temperature

and pressure and is used to inspect the atomic vibrations. In this comprehensive study, we have varied the temper- ature parameter from 0 to 800 K at different pressures values (0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, and 40 GPa). It is clear from the figure that α increases at low temperature up to 200 K and with increase in temperature approaches a small linear value. However, it is seen that α decreases dramatically with increase in pressure. As the pressure increases, the increase of α with temperature becomes smaller, especially at high temperatures.

From the self-polarized DFT approach, we have fore- casted electronic, magnetic, elasto-mechanical, thermo- electric, and thermal properties successfully. The lattice parameters at the cost of structural optimization show a decent aggregation with the experimental reported ones. Band structure and interpretation from the DOS empha- size semiconducting channels in both the spin cases. Elastic description of various moduli signifies the ductile capability of these alloys and hence aids for future tech- nological and industrial purposes. The high values of melting temperatures signify that both materials have the ability to retain their crystal structures over wide range of temperatures. Transport coefficients reveal the applicabil- ity of these actinide perovskites in semiconductor tech- nology and solid-state device applications. The performance of these complex materials on the basis of evaluated parameters gears its possibility towards energy harvesting technologies.

With the rapid growth of world energy requirement, a big challenge is to explore the light, safe, high energy density and environmental friendly energy sources for meeting the future energy market.1-8 It is well known that the metal dihydrides are attractive hydrogen storage materials because of their renewable, low cost, excellent deformation resistance, etc.9-15 Some noble metal hydrides have been investigated due to the good chemical stability and excellent catalytic activity.16-20 For example, the Pt-Ru catalyst shows high hydrogen generation rate.21 Ir-dopant can double enhance the hydrogen storage capacity of Pd nanoparticles.22 However, the main shortcomings of the noble metal storage hydrogen materials are the heavy den- sity and expensive cost.23 To solve these problems, MgH2 dihydride has been growing interest due to its low density,

We apply the first-principles calculations to study the structure, elastic modulus, Debye temperature and heat capacity of four TiH2. The results show that one new orthorhombic (Pnma) TiH2 is predicted. The tetragonal (I4mmm) TiH2 is more stable than the cubic (Fm-3m) TiH2. Compared to MgH2, TiH2 shows the strong deformation resistance. TiH2 dihydrides exhibit the strong bulk modulus compared to MgH2. The electronic structure shows that the high elastic modulus of TiH2 is determined by the Ti-H bonds. The Debye temperature of cubic (Fm-3m) and tetragonal (I4mmm) TiH2 is larger than the orthorhombic TiH2. The heat capacity follows the order of orthorhombic > cubic > tetragonal.

Among these transition metal hydrides, titanium hydrides (TiHx) are of great interest as the hydrogen stor- age materials because of high affinity to hydrogen, excel- lent catalytic activity and low cost.27,28 In particular, during the process of dehydrogenation, the stable and metastable titanium hydrides are benefit to form the hydrogen product and metal Ti. Recently, many titanium hydrides: ThH0.71, TiH and TiH2 have been found in Ti-H system. However, the structure and related properties of only titanium dihydride (TiH2) have been investigated due to the excellent dehydrogenation behavior.29,30 To our

knowledge, the overall properties such as catalytic activity, electronic properties and thermodynamic properties of a solid are influenced by the structural configuration.31-35 For TiH2, there has considerable controversy for its structure. Early work has been shown that there are two TiH2 phases: cubic (Fm-3m, No. 225) TiH2 36 and tetragonal (I4/mmm, No. 139) TiH2,37 respectively. Obviously, the reported crystal structure of TiH2 is different from the MgH2. Therefore, it is necessary to examine the structural stability of these TiH2 dihydride. In addition, the transportable capacity also plays an important role in hydrogen storage materials. The trans- portable capacity of a solid is estimated by the mechanical properties.38-41 Unfortunately, the mechanical properties of TiH2 are also unknown.

To explore the novel TiH2 hydrogen storage materials, in this paper, we use the first-principles calculations to study the structural stability, elastic modulus, Debye temperature and heat capacity of TiH2. Two novel TiH2 dihydrides: tetragonal (P42/mnm) and orthorhombic (Pnma) are con- sidered. Our work shows that one novel orthorhombic (Pnma) TiH2 is predicted. In particular, TiH2 exhibits strong

volume deformation resistance compared with the MgH2. In addition, the predicted orthorhombic (Pnma) TiH2 shows the high bulk modulus and shear modulus compared with the cubic and tetragonal TiH2 dihydrides.

For TiH2 dihydrides, the published phases are cubic (Fm-3m) and tetragonal (I4/mmm). The lattice parameter of a cubic structure is a = 4.535 Å.42 In this structure, Ti and H atoms occupy at the Wyckoff 4a(0, 0, 0) and 8c(0.25, 0.25, 0.25) sites, respectively. Another TiH2 dihydride belongs to the tetragonal structure. The lattice parameters of the tetrag- onal TiH2 are a = 3.202 Å and c = 4.279 Å,37 respectively. In this structure, Ti and H atoms occupy at the Wyckoff 2a (0, 0, 0) and 4d(0, 0.5, 0.25) sites, respectively. To explore the novel TiH2 dihydrides, we design two new structures: tetrag- onal (P42/mnm) and orthorhombic (Pnma), respectively. Figure 1 shows the structural model of four TiH2 dihydrides.

It is well known that the structural stability of the unknown phase is predicted by the first-principles calcu- lations.43-45 Hence, all calculations of TiH2 were calcu- lated by the first-principles calculations, as implemented in the CASTEP code.46,47 The exchange correlation func- tional of TiH2 dihydrides was used by the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) within Perdew-Burke- Ernzerhof (PBE) functional.48 The electronic configura- tions of Ti and H were 3p63d24s2 and 1s1, respectively. The interaction between the ionic and valence electron was treated by the ultrasoft pseudopotential.49 After conver- gence test, the energy cutoff for plane wave was selected to 400 eV and the k-point of TiH2 was 19 × 19 × 19 for cubic structure (Fm-3m), 18 × 18 × 21 for tetragonal structure (I4mmm), 11 × 11 × 16 for tetragonal structure (P42/mnm) and 10 × 16 × 9 for orthorhombic structure (Pnma), respectively. Total energy of a system was obtained by the density-mixing scheme in connection with the con- jugate gradient technique. The electronic energy toler- ance of the SCF was treated by the 1 × 10−6 eV/atom. During the structural optimization, all lattice parame- ters and atomic positions of a system were relaxed.50 The phonon dispersion of TiH2 was calculated by the Phonon code.51 The correlated calculated method was seen by the previous work.52

The stability of unknown phase are examined by the thermodynamically,53,54 as well as the dynamically.55 The thermodynamic stability of the TiH2 is examined by the formation enthalpy (ΔH),56,57 which is given by

Table 1 lists the calculated lattice parameters, volume, formation enthalpy and atomic coordinates of TiH2. It can be seen that the TiH2 dihydrides are thermodynamic stability because the calculated formation enthalpy of TiH2 is smaller than 0. In particular, the calculated for- mation enthalpy of the tetragonal structure (I4mmm: −5.067 eV/atom) is smaller than that of the cubic struc- ture (Fm-3m: −5.063 eV/atom), indicating that the tetrag- onal TiH2 is more thermodynamic stability than that of the cubic TiH2. In addition, we find that the calculated formation enthalpy of the predicted TiH2 is smaller than the known TiH2 dihydrides.

In addition to the thermodynamic stability, we should be examined the dynamical stability of TiH2 dihydrides. Generally, the no imaginary phonon frequency indicates the dynamical stability for a solid. To examine the dynamical stability, Figure 2 shows the calculated pho- non dispersion and phonon density of state (PhDOS) of TiH2. It is found that the cubic structure (Fm-3m), tetrag- onal structure (I4mmm) and orthorhombic structure (Pnma) TiH2 are dynamical stability because no imagi- nary phonon frequency is found in TiH2. However, we find that the tetragonal TiH2 is a dynamical instability, which is demonstrated by the phonon density of state. From Figure 2, the cubic (Fm-3m), tetragonal (I4mmm) and orthorhombic (Pnma) TiH2 are mechanical stability because of the positive frequencies in TiH2. However, the negative frequencies indicate that the tetragonal TiH2 is a mechanical instability. In particular, the high-temperature thermodynamic properties of TiH2 are contributed by the vibration of H atom. On the contrary, the low-temperature thermodynamic properties of TiH2 are contributed by the vibration of Ti atom. As mentioned above, we first predict one novel orthorhombic (Pnma) TiH2 dihydride.

Besides the structural stability, we should be further estimated the structural feature of the four TiH2 dihydrides. As shown in Table 1, we can see that the cal- culated lattice parameter of the cubic TiH2 is smaller than that of the Oadri and Skelton result.42 For tetragonal TiH2, the calculated value of a-axis is larger than that of
the Oadri and Skelton result. However, the calculated value of c-axis is smaller than that of the Oadri and Skel- ton result.37

Compared to cubic (Fm-3m) structure and tetragonal (I4mmm) structure, hydrogen atom in tetragonal (I4mmm) structure has a migration from 0.25 to 0.50. As a result, the migration of hydrogen changes the localized hybridization between Ti and H. Although there is one Ti-H bond both cubic (Fm-3m) structure and tetragonal (I4mmm) structure, the calculated Mulliken population of Ti-H bond for tetragonal structure (0.17) TiH2 is much larger than that of the cubic structure (0.08) TiH2. There is well explained why the tetragonal (I4mmm) TiH2 is more thermodynamic stability than that of the cubic (Fm-3m) TiH2.

For the predicted orthorhombic (Pnma) TiH2, the cal- culated lattice parameters are a = 5.148 Å, b = 2.862 Å and c = 5.684 Å, respectively. From Figure 1, it is found that the alternative stacking of Ti-H-Ti layers is distributed along the a-axis. Namely, the layered structure improves the stability of orthorhombic TiH2. For orthorhombic

TiH2, Ti occupies the Wyckoff (0.260, 0.250, 0.109) site, and H occupies the Wyckoff (0.5414, 0.750, 0.1771) and (0.1172, 0.750, 0.925) sites, respectively. Therefore, the structural feature forms three Ti-H bonds, which improve the structural stability of the orthorhombic TiH2.

As a hydrogen storage material, we must consider their mechanical properties to guarantee their trans- port.60-62 The mechanical properties of a solid are mea- sured by the elastic modulus: bulk modulus (B), shear modulus (G) and Young modulus (Y),63,64 respectively. The elastic modulus of hydrogen storage materials are calculated by the elastic constants (Cij).65-67

To explore the transportable effect of TiH2 dihydrides, Table 2 lists the calculated elastic constants of the TiH2 dihydrides. First, it is concluded that the TiH2 dihydrides are mechanical stability because the calculated elastic constants of the TiH2 dihydrides meet the Born stability criteria.68,69 Second, the calculated elastic constants C11 and C33 of TiH2 dihydrides are larger than that of the MgH2,70 indicating that the TiH2 dihydrides have strong deformation resistance along the a-axis and c-axis, respectively. On the other hand, the calculated elastic constant C11 of tetragonal (I4mmm) and orthorhombic (Pnma) TiH2 is larger than that of the elastic constant C33, implying that these TiH2 dihydrides have strong deformation resistance along the a-axis. It is suggested that the discrepancy derives from to the atomic distribution. Importantly, the calculated elastic constants C11 and C33 of orthorhombic (Pnma) TiH2 are 262.6 and 248.0 GPa, which are larger than that of the cubic (Fm-3m) and tetragonal (I4mmm) TiH2. The results indicate that the orthorhombic TiH2 has strong deformation resistance compared to the cubic (Fm-3m) and tetragonal (I4mmm) TiH2. The main reason is that our predicted orthorhombic TiH2 has strong local- ized hybridization between Ti and H.

Table 3 lists the calculated bulk modulus, shear mod- ulus, Young modulus and B/G ratio of the stable TiH2 dihydrides. It can be seen that the calculated bulk modu- lus of cubic (Fm-3m) TiH2 is 138.3 GPa, which is in good agreement with the experimental result.71 Although the calculated Young modulus of TiH2 is smaller than that of the MgH2, the calculated bulk modulus of TiH2 is larger than that of the MgH2. The results mean that TiH2 dihydrides have strong volume deformation resistance compared to the MgH2. In addition, the calculated shear modulus of the cubic TiH2 and tetragonal TiH2 is smaller than that of the MgH2. However, the calculated shear modulus of orthorhombic TiH2 is larger than that of the MgH2.70 In other words, the predicted orthorhombic TiH2 has strong shear deformation resistance compared

to the MgH2. In this paper, the calculated bulk modulus and shear modulus of the orthorhombic TiH2 are 139.5 and 51.5 GPa, respectively, which are larger than that of the cubic (Fm-3m) and tetragonal (I4mmm) TiH2. There- fore, we suggest that the predicted TiH2 dihydride has strong deformation resistances compared to cubic (Fm-3m) and tetragonal (I4mmm) TiH2.

The brittle-or-ductile behavior is an important parameter for the transportable capacity of the hydrogen storage mate- rials. Here, the brittle-or-ductile behavior of TiH2 dihydrides is measured by the Pugh method (B/G = 1.75).72,73 From Table 3, the calculated B/G ratio of the TiH2 dihydrides is larger than 1.75, implying that these TiH2 dihydrides show better ductility. The calculated B/G ratio of the cubic TiH2 is 10.65, which is larger than the tetragonal (I4mmm) and orthorhombic (Pnma) TiH2. It is suggested that the excel- lent ductility of the cubic TiH2 derives from the symmetri- cal Ti-H bond.

To study the electronic properties, Figure 3 shows the calculated band structure of TiH2 dihydrides along the high symmetry direction in the Brillouin zone. It can be seen that the TiH2 dihydrides exhibit the metallic behavior because some bands of all TiH2 across the EF. The calcu- lated electronic structure shows that the electronic proper- ties of the TiH2 dihydrides derive from the localized hybridization between Ti and H. Compared with the cubic structure, it is found that the band of tetragonal structure and orthorhombic structure occurs migration from the low energy region to the high energy region. As a result, the band shift can enhance the electronic interaction between the valence band and the conduction band.
Figure 4 shows the density of state (DOS) profiles of TiH2 dihydrides. It is found that the DOS profile of the TiH2 dihydrides across the EF, demonstrating that the

TiH2 dihydrides show the metallic behavior. Importantly, the DOS profiles of TiH2 dihydrides are contributed by the Ti-3d state and H-s state, respectively. For cubic structure, the DOS profile is mainly divided into two parts (see Figure 4A). The first part from −10.48 to −3.16 eV consists of H(s)-state, Ti(3d)-state and part of Ti(3p)-state. The last part from −3.16 to 4 eV mainly contains mixtures of Ti(3d)-state and part of Ti(3p)-state. Therefore, the localized hybridiza- tion between Ti and H forms the Ti-H bond in cubic struc- ture. The similar localized hybridization between Ti and H forms the Ti-H bond in other TiH2 structures.

Compared with the cubic (Fm-3m) and tetragonal (I4mmm) TiH2, there is a deep valley of the orthorhombic (Pnma) TiH2 near the EF. In particular, we find that the bands shift of orthorhombic structure occur migration from the low energy region to the high energy region. As a result, the DOS profile indicates the strong localized hybridization in orthorhombic TiH2, which forms the strong Ti-H bond compared to the cubic (Fm-3m) and tetragonal (I4mmm) structures.

Figure 5 shows the charge density distribution of three stable TiH2 dihydrides, while the critical feature is labeled. From Figure 5, it can be seen that there is an obvious electronic interaction between Ti and H, indicat- ing that the Ti-H bond is formed in TiH2 dihydrides. However, the nature of mechanical properties derives from the localized hybridization between Ti and H. Here, the calculated bond length of Ti-H bond is 1.917 Å for cubic structure (Fm-3m) TiH2 and 1.918 Å for tetragonal structure (I4mmm) TiH2, respectively. The bond length of Ti-H bond for cubic (Fm-3m) TiH2 is close to the tetrago- nal (I4mmm) TiH2. The value of population of Ti-H bond for tetragonal (I4mmm) TiH2 is larger than that of the cubic (Fm-3m) TiH2 because the overlap population of the tetragonal structure is stronger than that of the cubic structure.

Importantly, it is suggested that the chemical bonding of the orthorhombic (Pnma) TiH2 is different from the cubic (Fm-3m) and tetragonal (I4mmm) TiH2 due to the structural configuration. Compared with Figures 1 and 5,

there are three different Ti-H bonds because of its struc- tural configuration and the localized hybridization between Ti and H. Here, the calculated bond length of Ti-H bond is 1.907, 1.917 and 1.922 Å, respectively. On the other hand, the overlap population of orthorhombic structure is much stronger than that of the cubic structure and tetrago- nal structure. In particular, the Ti-H bonds are just distrib- uted in load applied, which improves the mechanical properties.

Finally, we study the thermodynamic properties of three stable TiH2 (cubic, tetragonal and orthorhombic). Here, we consider two important thermodynamic param- eters: Debye temperature (θD) and heat capacity (Cv), respectively.

Figure 6 shows the calculated Debye temperature and heat capacity of TiH2 dihydrides as a function of tempera- ture (0-2000 K). From Figure 6, it is found that the calcu- lated Debye temperature of TiH2 rapidly increases when

the temperature below 400 K. With increasing tempera- ture, the growth of Debye temperature is slow. The Debye temperature of cubic TiH2 is equal to the tetragonal TiH2. In particular, the calculated Debye temperature of the cubic and tetragonal TiH2 is larger than that of the ortho- rhombic TiH2. The phonon density of state shows that the low-temperature thermodynamic properties of TiH2 derive from the vibration of Ti. However, the high-temperature thermodynamic properties of TiH2 are attributed to the vibration of H atom.

On the other hand, we further investigate the heat capacity of TiH2. As shown in Figure 6, it is found that the calculated heat capacity of tetragonal TiH2 increases sharply (<1000 K). If the temperature is bigger than 1750 K, the heat capacity of tetragonal TiH2 is close to a constant. Here, the calculated heat capacity follows the order of ortho- rhombic structure>cubic structure>tetragonal structure. The calculated heat capacity of orthorhombic structure under high temperature is 69.21 J/mol K, which is larger than that of the other TiH2.

In summary, we apply the first-principles calculations to investigate the structure, elastic properties, Debye tem- perature and heat capacity of TiH2 hydrogen storage materials. Here, four TiH2 dihydrides: cubic (Fm-3m), tetragonal (I4mmm), tetragonal (P42/mnm) and ortho- rhombic (Pnma) structures are considered. We compare the elastic properties between TiH2 and MgH2.

The TiH2 dihydrides are thermodynamic stability because the calculated formation enthalpy is smaller than zero. The calculated formation enthalpy of tetragonal (I4mmm) TiH2 is smaller than that of the cubic (Fm-3m) TiH2. Based on the phonon dispersion curves, our predicted orthorhombic (Pnma) TiH2 is a dynamical stability. The cal- culated lattice parameters of the orthorhombic TiH2 are a = 5.148 Å, b = 2.862 Å and c = 5.684 Å, respectively.

The calculated elastic constants C11 and C33 of the TiH2 dihydrides are larger than that of the MgH2. Impor- tantly, the calculated bulk modulus and shear modulus of TiH2 dihydrides are larger than that of the MgH2. The TiH2 dihydrides have strong deformation resistance com- pared to the MgH2. The calculated bulk modulus and shear modulus of the orthorhombic (Pnma) TiH2 are 139.5 and 51.5 GPa, respectively, which are larger than that of the cubic (Fm-3m) and tetragonal (I4mmm) TiH2. The electronic structure shows that the high elastic modulus of TiH2 dihydrides derives from the formation of Ti-H bonds. The TiH2 dihydrides exhibit electronic properties due to the localized hybridization between Ti and H. The Debye temperature of the cubic and tetragonal TiH2 is larger than
the orthorhombic TiH2. The calculated heat capacity of TiH2 follows the order of orthorhombic>cubic>tetragonal.

Thermoelectric (TE) materials are in the center of world- wide research activities due to their ability to convert

Energy harvesting along with the thermoelectric materials has been investi- gated over recent decades with increased interest. This is not only due to their structural capability for demonstrating and integrating various new concepts to enhance the thermoelectric figure of merit but also high thermal stability, which is useful for thermoelectric devices. In the present investigation, we have used density functional theory combined with Boltzmann transport scheme to predict the properties of Co2XAl (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) Heuslers. The elastic parameters are simulated to determine the strength and ductile nature of these materials. Three different methods for exchange correlations are uti- lized to investigate the band profile for that modified Becke-Johnson potential illustrates the better results than generalized gradient approximation and GGA + U functional. The band profile found to be n-type (indirect band-gap) for Co2NbAl and p-type (direct band-gap) for Co2ZrAl and Co2HfAl Heuslers near the Fermi level. The formation and cohesive energy approve the thermo- dynamic stability of these materials. The band occupation and density of states in the post DFT treatment are used to predict the relations among various transport properties. The most important lattice portion of thermal conductiv- ity has been keenly determined by Slack's equation. The half-metallic nature along with efficient thermoelectric parameters, including electrical conductiv- ity, Seebeck coefficient, thermal conductivity, power factor, and zT suggest the likelihood of these materials to have a potential application in designing the shape of memory devices and imminent thermoelectric and energy harvesting materials.

Noteworthy momentum in the study of intermetal- lic Heusler alloys has increased over the last decade as these systems exhibit numerous extraordinary capabili- ties in showing the desired properties, extending from robust spin-polarization, half-metallic magnetism, mag- netoresistance, shape memory effect, spin gapless semi- conductor to giant magnetocaloric effect, phase transitions and TE effect. Systems include pnictides and related compounds,6 chalcogenides associated along with wurtzite configuration,7 and also new class of materials8-11 delivering half metallic character and bet- ter TE properties but the smart materials (Heuslers) achieving preferences over these systems because of their greater stability and high TE performance. Addi- tional motive to delegate Heusler alloys in these appli- cations is that these systems have the same crystallographic structure with different functional

characteristics and some of them are even very close in electronic structure and composition. Since the discov- ery of the NiMnSb Heusler alloy in 1983, a sequence of experimental as well as theoretical efforts (first princi- ples simulations) were attempted to predict novel semi- conductor or half-metallic systems. Among such compounds, transition metal-based Heuslers have been widely investigated by material scientists worldwide. Predominantly, the Co-based Heusler structures consti- tute a vast family with semiconducting or half-metallic band profiles.

The high TE performance signified by Bi2Te3, Bi2Se3, and Sb2Te3 can be recognized by delivering the high PF possessing significant carrier concentration and low κ fetched from the structure by the weakly bounded van der Waals interaction. Newly, doped Heusler Fe2V0.8W0.2Al prepared possessing zT = 6,12 hence Heuslers become the vital part as they have become the point of prestige in TE research because of due to the semiconducting performance and most important the tunable band-gaps. The recent experi- mental study in the field of thin films of Heuslers including Cr2CoGa,13 Co2MnGe,14 Co2FeAl,15 Fe2CoSi,16 Fe2CrGa,17 Co2MnSi,18 Co2FeSn19 and Cu2MnAl, Co2MnSi, Co2MnGe and Co2MnSn20 also possesses some novel properties. Motivated by above- mentioned striking properties and keeping in view the multi-dimensional applications, we have carried out Co2XAl (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) Heuslers. Therefore, the main aim of this present study is to investigate the TEs (con- version of waste heat into electricity), half-metallicity and mechanical properties and of Co-based Heuslers. The present work will overcome the lack of available data for these materials and will provide as reference data, which can serve as a tool for further advance in experimental as well as theoretical studies.

The density functional theory (DFT) has proved a remarkable theory due to its remarkable description provided about the ground state properties in bulk as well as surfaces and specifically a large number of materials has been investigated. The piece of work was achieved by using full potential linearized augmented plane wave method as executed in WEIN2k code.21 Leading term exchange-correlation is generally projec- ted from different methods such as generalized gradient schemes (GGA) of Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE).22 The electronic exchange and correlation effects were performed with the GGA of PBE. In order to study the

on-site correlation at the 3D transition metals, the GGA + U method were used. In the GGA + U scheme, the effective Coulomb-exchange parameter Ueff = U – J should be used where U is the Coulomb part (Hubbard U) and J is the exchange part.23. The Ueff = U – J where U is the on-site Coulomb interaction was fixed such that U = 0.40 Ry and J varies from 0 to 0.05 eV for the present set of alloys. As GGA underestimates band gap for systems with d/f electrons hence to overcome the problem, the modified Becke-Johnson (mBJ) potential and Hubbard potential are also used for present analy- sis. However, some advanced approach mBJ24 is used predominately for particularly correlated systems. How- ever, the exactness of mBJ potential is more to deliver the ground state properties of a material, this is due to because of highly correlated electron systems does not provide the precise description by GGA. The muffin-tin radii (RMT) are set to prevent electron charge leakage within the interstitial sites. The wave function inside sphere is extended up to lmax = 12 and RMTkmak = 7 was set for the present alloys, where RMT is the smallest atomic sphere radius in the unit cell and kMAX is the magnitude of the largest k vector. For self-consistent calculation, we have used 2000 k-mesh points to obtain better convergence. For the present set of alloys, the total charge, and energy convergence has been set at 10−4 e and 10−7 eV respectively. Elastic constants are fetched by using cubic-elastic code for the present set of alloys.25 By using the calculation for band occupation, the Boltzmann transport theory is used to figure out the transport coefficients.26 Seebeck tensors, electrical con- ductivity, and the group velocity can be determined as following relations expressed as:

A structural property defines the crucial role in under- standing the occupation of atoms in their respective posi- tions. Structural parameters are obtained using the calculation of energy in different structural phases of Co2XAl (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) Heuslers. All possible cubic crystal configurations are taken into consideration with specifically two structural prototypes as Cu2MnAl with space group (#225) and with the Hg2CuTi (#216). The conforming atomic sites are Co (0.75, 0.75, 0.75), X (0.50, 0.50, 0.50), and Al (0, 0, 0) for Cu2MnAl type and Co- atoms occupy 4d (0, 0, 0) and 4b (1/4, 1/4, 1/4) sites, X on 4c (1/2, ½, ½) and Al on 4a (3/4, 3 / 4, 3 / 4) for Hg2CuTi-type. The ground state energy optimization prototype struc- tures define the Cu2MnAl as the stable one shown in Figure 1 for Co2Xal (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) Heuslers.

The elastic constants Cij are fundamental and indis- pensable for describing the mechanical properties of materials, which can be obtained from ground state total energy calculations. These constants can be used to check the mechanical stability of the studied compounds and are linked thermodynamically to the specific heat, ther- mal expansion, Debye temperature, and Grüneisen parameter.27,28 Moreover, they can provide an estimation of the strength and indirectly the melting temperature. Macroscopic distortion of a crystal structure is directly related to the elastic constants and is applicable in the evaluation of elastic energies or strains in materials under applied (internal/external/thermal) stresses.29 These constants are determined by the linear response of a crystal towards the external forces, and are also associ- ated with structural stability, equation of state (EOS) interatomic potential and phonon spectra. Consequently, the determination of elastic constants is necessary to characterize a solid crystal. To further discuss the mechanical stability of these alloys, the elastic constants have been computed from cubic-elastic package. If a sys- tem is arbitrary deformed from equilibrium conditions through small strain “ei,” the change in energy would be P 6

The cubic symmetric system requires only C11, C12, and C44. This

The requirement on these elastic constants are C11 > 0, C12 > 0, C44 > 0, (C11 - C12) > 0, and C12 < B < C11 defined by Born-Haung.30,31 For Co2XAl (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) alloys, the second-order elastic constants satisfies the said circumstances, approving the stability of these alloys and is displayed in Table 1. Young's modulus, or the Young modulus, is a mechanical property that measures the stiffness of a solid material. It defines the relationship between stress (force per unit area) and strain (proportional deforma- tion) in a material in the linear elasticity regime of a uniaxial deformation. The calculated values of Young's modulus of these alloys indicating they are stiff in nature.

The Poisson's ratio (υ) is another factor used to sepa- rate the materials via ductile or brittle.32 (υ) also desig- nates the nature and bonding forces preserved in the material. If its value is >0.26 the material retains ductile nature otherwise the material acts as a brittle. (υ) also delivers the evidence about the bonding forces existing in the materials. For central force in the solids, the Poisson's ratio has a boundary of 0.25 to 0.5. From our calculated values (υ) lies in this range, suggests that the bonding

forces are of central type for these alloys. Pugh's ratio B/G is closely related to the brittle and ductile nature of materials and thus, highlighted a significant relation between the elastic and plastic properties of pure poly- crystalline metals. If B/G > 1.75, then the material is duc- tile while as brittle materials are characterized by B/G < 1.75.33 The covalent materials in principle are rel- atively hard and obviously brittle with a smaller Pugh ratio. The strong covalent bonds in such materials cer- tainly produce a significant resistance resulting in hard- ness. Conversely, ductile materials with a high Pugh's ratio are characterized by metallic bonding and low hard- ness. Therefore, the calculated values show that present set of alloys are ductile in nature. The nature of the bond- ing of cubic systems can also be explained in terms of their Cauchy pressure.34 Materials with positive value of Cauchy pressure holds the ductility character, otherwise the negative value reflects the brittle character of a mate- rial. Positive Cauchy pressure also specifies the presence of metallic bonding in a material while as the negative value demonstrates the directional and angular bonds. In the present set of calculations, Cauchy pressure predicted for all Heusler alloys are positive which reflects the duc- tile character.

Elastic anisotropy (A) outlines a crucial role in defin- ing the micro-cracks at growing process.35 If A = 1, then the crystal is prescribed to be completely isotropic, if the values lies below the unity signifies elastic anisotropy. It has been found that almost all crystalline materials exhibit anisotropic nature. The value of A diverges from unity and hence Co2XAl (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) alloys exhibit anisotropic behavior which may result in structural deformation or micro cracks during growing process.

mBJ, and on-site GGA + U has been utilized to predict the electronic nature of Co2XAl (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) Heuslers along high-symmetry Brillion zone (BZ) is represented in Table 3. The materials possessing smart magneto- electronic profile are immensely required in numerous scientific fields. Therefore, nature of magneto-electronic properties of such alloys is quite necessary. By employing GGA formalism, it clearly portrays half-metallic nature. As we know that the transition metal systems are usually highly correlated, so further elucidate of this discrepancy has to be needed. Since the GGA method underestimates the band gap, so we have incorporated mBJ and on-site Hubbard-parameter (U) method to GGA in order to obtain the precise band structure. So, in order to eliminate the vagueness, the GGA + U method has been adopted. The current value of U was precisely chosen for Co-d orbital electrons is 5.98 eV. However, the Hubbard correc- tion is insufficient for these Heuslers. So, we have employed mBJ potential to define effective and accurate band profile. The key benefit of the mBJ is the inbuilt potential due to which the accurate examination of the band gap energies and have been investigated for Co2XAl (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) Heuslers and is illustrated in Figure 3. The origin of half-metallic nature of Co2XAl (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) Heuslers can be explored by presenting the possible hybridization among the constituent atoms schematically. The transition metal atom d-states in presence of crystal field are decomposed into double degenerate for example, (dx 2 –y 2, dz 2) and triple degenerate t2g (dxy, dyz, dzx) states. The appearance band gap in the minority spin state and half-metallicity in Heusler compounds originates from d– d hybridization of transition metal atoms.

The total DOS is illustrated in the Figure 4 expresses the consequence of mBJ potential mainly on the elec- tronic profiles. The different energy states are shifted pre- dominantly from the Fermi level offers of band gap there. Further the clarification of the energy states which are primarily linked with the bands (ie, to analyses the visibil- ity of the states), we have plotted partial density of states. The transition element Co-atom contributes more as dis- played in Figure 5A-F than other elements. Whereas, properties of X = (Zr/Nb/Hf) and Al states are typically far from the valance band, thus do not perform any signif- icant character in determining the electronic profile that is, their contribution of magnetic character is least around the Fermi level. The d-electron dominates the electronic profile of the alloys. On comparing the pDOS of the trio alloys, we examine the d-states of transition atoms through Fermi level delivers half metallic character of alloys. In Co-based alloy, both dt2g as well deg-states are below Fermi signifies in p-d hybridization in up-spin channel. However, in down-spin dt2g-states are at Fermi level while deg states are empty lie above Fermi level. The d-states are unevenly dispersed giving rise to the

magnetism of alloys. The positive magnetic moment of the various atoms hints that the interaction of spins aligns in the same direction and negative moments convey anti- ferro or ferrimagnetic interactions. The integral magnetic moment which is the characteristic feature of the half- metallicity of the Heusler alloys. From the Table 4, it is seen that the atoms having positive sign indicates the fer- romagnetic conformation of spins with respect to each other. The overall combination of ferromagnetic spins constitutes the net magnetism in their corresponding structures. Hence, the sufficient magnetism containing these Heuslers may lend their extending stand in high performance spin electronic devices that is, spintronic, shape memory alloys, spin injectors, and so on.
The description of electronic charge density precisely depicts better understanding about the nature of chemical bonding and has been predominantly used for the charge

distraction. However, it includes the effect of non-bonding states and gives the overall charge density. For the alloys under investigation, the charge density contour plots are shown in Figure 6. In these plots, the charge shearing among the constituent atoms is well distinguished by color difference that changes around the atoms. From the two electron density plots, we can see that the transition metals shear maximum contribution in contrast to p group ele- ments. The charge density plots that basically act as indica- tor between the bonding of various constituents in the crystal structures. From this plot, it is obvious that the shape of s-p element in these alloys is not completely spherical indicating the mixed nature of bonds which can also be verified by difference in electronegativity of s,p

atom with other transition metals because electronegativity is also a basic factor for determining the nature of bonds. The electronegativity of Co, Zr/Nb/Hf, and Al atoms are 1.91, 1.33/1.60/1.30 and 1.61 with units on Pauling scale, respectively. Therefore, it is clear from the charge density plot that the nature of bonding in these alloys has mixture of covalent as well as ionic bonding and hence polar cova- lent bonding is preserved within their crystal lattices.
The surge in energy consumption and environmental protection require more efficient and clean technologies

for the energy conversion and utilization. The concept of TE seems to be one of the solutions for both these problems and is becoming an alternate source of energy. The TE conversion technique based on the Seebeck effect, which has many advantages, that is, environment-friendly, non-moving parts, and direct uti- lization of low-grade heat energy, has attracted exten- sive attention in recent years.37,38 TE effect is designated as the reverse of squander heat into

electrical energy that is, thermal-to-electric energy by using the Seebeck effect to make a way for sustainable energy technology and to overcome the energy crisis. Those materials, which convert heat energy into electri- cal energy, were called as TE materials.39,40

Next, we calculated the carrier concentrations at dif- ferent ranges of temperatures for Co2XAl (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) alloys is plotted in Figure 8. As the temperature is increased, the number of broken bonds (carriers) increases because there is more thermal energy available so more and more electrons gain enough energy to break free. Each electron that makes it to the conduction band leaves behind a hole in the valence band and there is an increase in both the electron and hole concentration. As

the temperature is decreased, electrons do not receive enough energy to break a bond and remain in the valence band. If electrons are in the conduction band, they will quickly lose energy and fall back to the valence band, annihilating a hole. Therefore, lowering the temperature causes a decrease in the intrinsic carrier concentration, while raising the temperature causes an increase in intrinsic carrier concentration. Here, in the preset set of alloys, in spin-up channel, we can see that electrons are the majority charge carriers. The carrier concentration shows a linear decay for Co2ZrAl, Co2NbAl shows an increase at higher temperatures and Co2HfAl show a lin- ear rise in temperature. In spin-down channel, holes are the majority carriers where a negligible change up to room temperature is seen in the present set of the alloys.

Figure 9 displays the electrical conductivity (σ/τ) devi- ation with temperature. One can observe that with the rise in temperature the electrical conductivity also shows inclination trend. It is due to the reason that rises in carrier concentration the σ also increases at higher tem- perature. The carrier concentration and electrical con- ductivity are interrelated by the mathematical equation σ = neμ, where μ is the mobility. Positive temperature dependency at high temperature of σ/τ is because of increasing carrier concentration.

the carrier concentration plays a prominent character in determining the overall thermal conductivity. The larger the number of carriers, the higher will be the thermal conductivity. However, for the spin minority state, the magnitude of thermal conductivity is large as compared with the spin up state; it is because of the presence of a large number of carriers in the metallic channel. Recently, Co2MnAs alloy predicted with a PF 0.40 × 10−5 W/mK2 at 0 K and 0GPa. Enamullah et al evalu- ate PF of Co-based Heuslers nearly equal to 0.80 × 10−5 W/mK2 at room temperature. However, Sofi et al explored the PF of approximately 1.20 W/mK2 for

Co2ScSb and 1.80 W/mK2 for Co2TiSb at 0 K and 0GPa. On comparing the PF of above said materials, the current study delivers a significant PF as illustrated in Figure 11A. At 0GPa and 0 K the predicted PF for Co2XAl (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) is 2.95 × 10−5 W/mK2, 4.72 × 10−5 W/mK2, 6.38 × 10−5 W/mK2, respectively. The present set of Heuslers demonstrates the value of PF is high in comparison with the Co-based Heuslers at 0 K and 0 GPa. Thus, we conclude that Co2XAl (X = Zr, Nb,
Hf) Heuslers shows a good PF and lends its possibility in TEs.

Figure of merit (zT) performance of Co2XAl (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) Heuslers has been projected through Seebeck coef- ficient, thermal, electrical transport data in 50 to 800 range of temperature. From Figure 11B the obtained value of zT for Co2ZrAl at 600 K is 0.62, Co2NbAl at 500 K is 0.77 Co2HfAl at 450 K is 0.8. Hence, we conclude that Hf > Nb > Zr therefore, Co2HfAl is best among them.

Using ab-initio density functional and the Boltzmann transport theory, we present a systematic study which correctly predicts the magneto-electronic, elasto- mechanical and TE properties of Co2XAl (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) Heuslers. The representation of density of states and band profile indicates the half-metallic nature in of Co2Xal (X = Zr, Nb, Hf) alloys. The band-gap calculated from the observed band structures was found to be indi- rect having n-type for Co2NbAl Heusler and p-type for Co2ZrAl and Co2HfAl with direct band-gap near Fermi level. The strongly dependent elastic constants illustrate the ductile feature of these alloys. Predominately, the electrical and thermal conductivities were found greatly increasing with increasing temperature, typically in their semiconducting nature. Lattice thermal conductiv- ity can be reduced further by the different mechanism (eg, extrinsic/intrinsic defects and external doping) which certainly enhance zT value. The significant value of Seebeck coefficient, PF, figure of merit and lattice thermal conductivity at higher temperature enables the potential of these alloys to find a possible way in spintronic technology and TE power generation appli- cations. Therefore, from our calculated results for

Co2Xal (X = Zr, Nb, Hf), Heuslers will deliver a new route to our experimentalists for the validification experimentally of the predicted alloys. Therefore, future studies should be carried out to enhance the thermo- power of these materials and to expense the waste heat (temperature gradient) properly into usable electric power.

1 Introduction The iron–gallium alloy systems (Galfenol) have appeared excellent performance as candi- dates for giant magnetostrictive material applied in sensors, transducers, and actuators. They offer desirable properties including excellent tensile strengths and magnetostrictive strains [1–3]. What is more, as the most promising magnetostrictive material, Fe–Ga alloys have shown numer- ous advantages such as excellent ductility, low saturation magnetic ﬁeld, and low associated cost [4–7]. In the past decades, researchers mainly focused on the improving of magnetostriction coefﬁcients, the concentration effect of gallium element, and the single crystal preparation method.

Closely associated with various fundamental solid-state properties such as equation of state, hardness, and phonon spectra, elastic properties are critical for researchers to get a good understanding of the “temper” of a material.

increasing temperature. In addition, the three types Fe3Ga are mechanically stable at room temperature and maintain ductility nature with increasing temperature. However, it should be noted that the DO3 type Fe3Ga is more sensitive to temperature, while the elastic properties of L12 and DO19 type Fe3Ga exhibit a very gentle changing trend with increasing temperature. This indicates that L12 and DO19 type Fe3Ga can keep their mechanical properties through wide temperature range and have good temperature stability. In contrast, for Fe3Ga in DO3 structure, the elastic properties are not as stable as the L12 and DO19 structures when temperature is higher than 475 K.

Continuous-wave measurement of the shear elastic con- stants of bcc Fe–Ga solid solutions shows that the constant C44 is independent of the gallium composition while the constant (C11–C12)/2 decreases linearly and extrapolates to zero at around 26 at.% Ga [8–10]. The magnetostrictive coefﬁcient of Fe–Ga alloy also reaches a peak value at a Ga content of about 27.5 at.%, conﬁrming a close relation between the elastic properties and the magnetostrictive coefﬁcient. Hence, the study on the elastic properties of Fe–Ga alloy will be signiﬁcant not only for understanding its magnetostriction property, but also for designing new alloys. At present, the gallium content and magnetic ﬁeld dependence of Fe–Ga alloy elastic properties have been studied very well by researchers, but the temperature- dependent elastic properties of Fe–Ga alloys were given little attention. Based on the above discussion, investigation
on the effect of the temperature on the elastic properties is critical for the understanding of Fe–Ga magnetostrictive alloys.

In the recent years, a number of studies of elastic and thermodynamic properties at ﬁnite temperature have been reported. Experimentally, the investigation of temperature- dependent elastic properties can be carried out by using the resonant ultrasound spectroscopy (RUS) [11] method. Nevertheless, experimental determination of the elastic constants at elevated temperature has always been chal- lenging because the results may be disputed by external factors. With the development of the high temperature elastic theories and the computing techniques, researchers have developed a new method to investigate the elastic properties at ﬁnite temperature. Wang et al. [12] proposed a quasistatic approach to study the temperature-dependent elastic properties by using ﬁrst-principles method with DFT. This approach is based on the fact that the temperature dependence of elastic constants mainly results from volume expansion with increasing temperature. By using Wang’s method, several groups have predicted the correspond- ing temperature-dependent elastic properties successfully [13–18]. Wang et al. [12] performed ﬁrst-principles calculations on B2-MgRE intermetallic compounds to predict their temperature-dependent elastic properties. Ganeshan [18] calculated the elastic coefﬁcient and thermodynamic properties of MgX (X ¼ Si, Ge, Sn, Pb) with the ﬁrst-principles approach. So far as we know, no theoretical calculations about the temperature-dependent elastic properties of Fe–Ga system have been reported in the literature. Motivated by the speciﬁc interests of magne- tostrictive material Fe–Ga, calculations of the elastic and thermodynamic properties at ﬁnite temperature of Fe–Ga are performed by using the ﬁrst-principles calculations combined with quasi-harmonic approximations (QHA). The mechanical stability and the thermodynamic properties of different structure type Fe3Ga alloys are discussed based on the calculations. The present study would be a good reference for further experimental measurements of the elastic constants at ﬁnite temperature of Fe–Ga alloy.

2.1 Details of ﬁrst-principles and phonon calculations In the present calculations, three proto- type structures of Fe3Ga alloys have been adopted: BiF3-prototype structure (DO3), AuCu3-prototype structure (L12), and Ni3Sn-prototype structure (DO19). The corre- sponding crystal information has been listed in Table 1. One can see that the calculated lattice parameters are in good agreement with experimental values. The calculations were performed by Cambridge Serial Total Energy Package (CASTEP) [21] which based on the density functional theory (DFT). The GGA [22] with PBE functional is used for the exchange correlation of electrons and the ultrasoft pseudopotentials are employed. The kinetic energy cut-off of 530 eV was determined to guaranteeing the convergence of total energies within an accuracy of 10 7 eV/atom. In

order to test the accuracy of our choice for the cutoff energy upon the total energies, calculations were performed using a cutoff energy of 630 eV for the Fe–Ga alloys. The ﬂuctuation for the total energy is less than 1%, which proved that 430 eV is sufﬁcient to calculate the total energy accurately. The Monkhorst–Pack k-point meshes [23] with a smearing value of 0.1 eV for the electronic levels were used. The k-meshes were 16 16 16 for DO3-type and L12-type Fe–Ga, and 13 13 15 for DO19-type. Since high accuracy is needed to evaluate the elastic constants, the convergence of ﬁnal energies with respect to the k-point meshes was carefully checked.

Magnetic ordering plays an important role in 3d transition metal like Fe. For example, in Fe3Ga (DO3) structure, there are two different types of Fe atoms (FeІ and FeII). Thus, there will be four different magnetic arrange- ments, (FeІ)"#(FeII)"#. Naturally, each metal atom may exhibit a high-spin or a low-spin solution. So for Fe3Ga (DO3), there will be 16 possible magnetic conﬁgurations. Fortunately, we can reduce the numbers by considering the fact that Fe3Ga compounds are ferrimagnetic (FRM). Therefore, the ferrimagnetic ordering was taken as starting point for the Fe3Ga alloys. We performed calculations for the two conﬁgurations with consideration of the spin-states. In order to verify the accuracy of our settings of the spin polarization, we compare our results of the magnetic moments with other investigators. Our calculated magnetic moments of the Fe3Ga (DO3) structure are 2.46mB for FeІ and 1.96mB for FeII, which agrees well with the literature results, 2.41mB for FeІ and 1.96mB for FeII.

The magnetic moment as a function of the volume are plotted and shown in Fig. 1. As can be seen from Fig. 1, with the volume shrinking, the magnetic moment of Fe is dropping fast. For L12 and DO19 structure, there is a sharp decline in its magnetic moment when the volume shrinks to 95% of the equilibrium volume. However, for the DO3

structure, the sharp decline happened when the volume shrinks to 80% of the equilibrium volume. The sharp decline implies that the magnetic order has nearly collapsed. This is because the vacancy in the spin-down state are occupied by electrons when the volume is shrinking, and the increase in the number of occupying electrons in spin-down state is greater than the number of occupying electrons in spin-up
state, thus the magnetic moment showing a decreasing trend with the shrinking volume.

Phonon calculations for Fe3Ga are performed by using the ﬁnite displacement method, which gives a supercell of 64 atoms for L12-type, DO3-type, and DO19-type Fe3Ga. The Brillion zone sampling was set as an 8 8 8 k-point mesh for the PDOS calculations. Figure 2 shows the phonon dispersion curves of the L12-type, DO3-type, and DO19-type Fe3Ga. Evidently, there is no imaginary frequency, which shows the dynamical stability of Fe3Ga. Although no experimental and theoretical data are available for comparison, the thermal expansion coefﬁcient evaluated from the present phonon calculations are in good accordance with experimental results. What is more, the phonon dispersion curves of FeAl were calculated in the same method to verify the accuracy of our phonon calculations, as shown in Fig. 2(d). The calculated curves are in agreement with experimental results [24], which showed that the present phonon calculations are reliable.

where sij is the stress tensor, Cijkl is the elastic constant tensor which is a 6 6 matrix, and ekl represents the Lagrangian strain tensor. In different crystal structure, the diversity of symmetry could result in some tensors equal and others equal to 0. According to the structure symmetry of L12-type and DO3-type Fe3Ga (cubic system), it has three independent elastic constants, C11, C12, and C44. So Eq. (5) can be written in a simpliﬁed form as:
where Cij are the elastic constants, si and ti is the normal stress and shear stress, and ei, gi are the normal strain and shear strain, respectively.
