where

In order to get the elastic constants as a function of temperature, we use a quasistatic approach developed by Wang [12]. In the light of this approach, our calculations are divided into three steps. First, the equilibrium volume V(T) at a given temperature is calculated by using the quasi- harmonic approximation approach (QHA). Second, elastic constants at 0 K as a function of volume V, Cij(V) are obtained. In the third step, the calculated elastic constants from the second step are approximated as those at ﬁnite temperature. In order to be comparable with measured data, the isothermal elastic constants must be transformed to the isentropic elastic constants by
where Cv is the isochoric heat capacity and a is the thermal expansion coefﬁcient.

3.1 Thermal expansion As an important physical property of the materials, the thermal expansion can be used to study the various issues of related materials. Togo [30] demonstrates phonon properties with fundamental equations and shows examples how the phonon calculations are applied in calculating thermal expansion. By Vient EOS, the equilibrium volume V as a function of temperature are obtained and shown in Fig. 4(a). Obviously the equilibrium volume of the three types Fe3Ga increases with increasing temperature. From the V–T relationship, the thermal expansion property can be easily obtained. Figure 4(b) shows our calculated temperature-dependent linear thermal expansion coefﬁcient (a, LTEC) of L12-type, DO3-type, and DO19-type Fe3Ga together with available experimental data from dilatometry method by Zhang et al. [31]. Figure 4(c) shows the thermal expansion (Dl/l) of L12-type Fe3Ga from

X-ray analysis by Kawamiya et al. [19]. Clearly, the calculated thermal expansion is in good agreement with experimental results, which validated the reasonability of the thermodynamic results calculations presented in this work.

From Fig. 4(a), one can see that the linear thermal expansion coefﬁcient exhibits an increase with temperature, and the increase trend is eventually smaller at high temperature. For DO3-Fe3Ga, obviously, the LTEC (a) of DO3-type Fe3Ga is higher than the L12 and DO19, and the discrepancy increases with temperature increasing. This is because the bulk modulus of DO3-Fe3Ga is smaller than L12 and DO19 Fe3Ga, as clearly shown in Fig. 4(d). What is more, the curve slope of bulk modulus of DO3-Fe3Ga is much larger than L12 and DO19 Fe3Ga, which explains the increasing discrepancy of LTEC (a) between them. In addition, The LTEC of L12 and DO19 type Fe3Ga is close to each other, which has an average value of 12.26 10 6 and 12.77 10 6 K 1 between 300 and 800 K, respectively. The experimental a of L12-Fe3Ga from Kawamiya is 12.3

0.4 10 6 K 1, which matches perfect with our calculated results. From Fig. 4(d), we can see that the bulk modulus of DO19-Fe3Ga is a little higher than L12-Fe3Ga, which is in good accordance with the LTEC (a) results.

3.2 Temperature-dependent elastic properties Theinvestigation of temperature-dependent elastic properties of alloys and compounds are essential for us to understand the mechanism of mechanical stability, strength, as well as phase transitions. The calculated temperature-dependent isentropic elastic constants CS 11, CS 12, and CS 44 are shown in Fig. 5, together with corresponding experimental values from Clark et al. [32]. Obviously, all three elastic constants monotonically decrease with the increasing temperature, which is consistent with the general feature of thermo- elasticity for solid materials. From Fig. 5(a), one can see that there is a little discrepancy between our calculated results and experimental ones, which may be resulted from the appearance of A2 phase in the slow-cooled Fe3Ga samples. Furthermore,theCS 11 hasthelargestdescendingrate,implying that the axial compression resistance decreases obviously and the resistance to shear deformation is reduced. Interestingly, the descending rate of CS 11 of DO3-type Fe3Ga is much larger than L12 and DO19 type Fe3Ga. It intersects with CS 12 and CS 44 at the temperature of 475 and 600 K, respectively. Thus, we concluded that the resistance to shear deformation of L12 and DO19 type Fe3Ga is stable with the increasing temperature. For DO3 type Fe3Ga, the resistance to shear deformation dropped dramatically over the temperature of 475 K.

The temperature dependent shear modulus (G), quotient of shear to bulk modulus (G/B), Young’s modulus (E), and Poisson’s ratio (n) are further calculated from the obtained isentropic elastic constants, and the results are shown in Fig. 6. The overall observation is that both the shear modulus and Young’s modulus of the three types of Fe3Ga decrease with increasing temperature. The shear modulus G represents the resistance to plastic deformation (bond-angle change) and relates to the hardness of a material. Generally said, the larger the G, the harder the material. The Young’s modulus E represents the stiffness degree of the material. The larger the Young’s modulus is, the stiffer the material is. From Fig. 6(a) and (c), the shear modulus G and Young’s modulus E of DO3-Fe3Ga has a larger descending rate than L12 and DO19 type Fe3Ga, which is in agreement with the changing trend of the bulk modulus BT. Furthermore, the G/B value plotted in Fig. 6(d) showed that the G/B of DO3-Fe3Ga decrease fast with temperature, which means that temperature can improve the ductility of DO3-Fe3Ga. Because a low G/B value (less than 0.5) is associated with ductility and a high value (greater than 0.5) is associated with brittleness. But for the L12 and DO19 type Fe3Ga, differently, one can see that both the shear modulus G, G/B value, and Young’s modulus E are not sensitive to the temperature, which means temperature has little effect on the hardness property of L12 and DO19 type Fe3Ga. Poisson’s ratio (n) is the elastic constant reﬂects the lateral deformation of the material. As can be seen from Fig. 6(d),
the Poisson’s ratio (n) of DO3-Fe3Ga increases with the increasing of temperature linearly, which means the lateral deformation become larger with the increasing temperature.
However, the Poisson’s ratio (n) of L12 and DO19 type Fe3Ga, just like the Young’s modulus E, is insensitive to the temperature.

4 Conclusions In summary, the temperature-depen- dent elastic and thermodynamic properties of Fe3Ga with L12, DO3, and DO19 structure have been performed by ﬁrst-principles calculations combined with quasi-harmonic approximation method. Excellent corresponding among our calculations and the experimental results validates the reasonability of the present work. Obviously, tempera- ture has signiﬁcant effect on elastic and thermodynamic properties such as volume thermal expansion, elastic constants, shear and bulk modulus, etc. Interestingly, Fe3Ga with DO3 structure is more sensitive to temperature than L12 and DO19 type Fe3Ga, revealing the metastable nature of DO3 type Fe3Ga. For Fe3Ga with L12 and DO19 structure, they exhibit as stable phase under the condition of increasing temperature. The present work is expected to provide helpful references for subsequent experimental and
theoretical study of magnetostrictive material iron–gal- lium. Furthermore, clues for designing iron–gallium based materials and devices are expected to be given by our study.

\begin{title}
First-principles studies of typical long-period superstructures Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti in Al-rich TiAl alloys
\end{title}

Ping-Ying Tang a,b, Bi-Yu Tang a,c,⇑, Xu-Ping Su c

a School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Guangxi University, Nanning 530004, China b College of Physics and Electronic Engineering, Guangxi Teachers Education University, Nanning 530001, China c School of Mechanical Engineering, Xiangtan University, Hunan Province 411105, China

\begin{title}
a r t i c l e i n f o
\end{title}

Article history: Received 21 September 2010 Received in revised form 29 November 2010 Accepted 1 December 2010 Available online 24 December 2010

Keywords: LPSs First-principles calculations Structural stabilities Electronic structures Elastic properties

\begin{title}
1. Introduction
\end{title}

As potential candidates for high temperature applications, Ti–Al based intermetallic compounds have been under extensive exper- imental and theoretical studies. These Ti–Al intermetallics have promising properties including excellent elevated-temperature strength, resistance to oxidation and corrosion, relatively low den- sity and high melting point. Compared to Ti-rich alloys, Al-rich TiAl alloys have lower densities and better oxidation resistance due to the formation of protective alumina scales in place of Titanium oxi- des [1]. Therefore, study on Al-rich TiAl alloys has been attractive and needs to be carried out very deeply.

Several Al-rich phases with various long-period superstructures (LPSs) such as Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti, r-Al2Ti, h-Al11Ti5, h-Al5Ti2 and Al3Ti have been observed in the Ti–Al system [2–22]. Among these LPSs, Al5Ti3 (Ga5Ti3-type), h-Al2Ti (Ga2Zr-type) and r-Al2Ti (Ga2Hf-type) are justly on the Al-rich side next to the c-TiAl single-phase. Al5Ti3 was ﬁrst observed in Ti-63 at.% Al annealed at 700 C by Miida et al. [2]. Subsequently, it has frequently been conﬁrmed by various more recent electron microscopy studies on rapidly quenched con- ventionally cast, and/or low temperature annealed (below about 800 C) TiAl alloys in this composition range [3–16]. Metastable

⇑Corresponding author at: School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Guangxi University, Nanning 530004, China. Tel.: +86 732 8292195; fax: +86 732 8292468.

E-mail address: tangbiyu@gxu.edu.cn (B.-Y. Tang).

\begin{title}
a b s t r a c t
\end{title}

First-principles calculations are performed to study the structural stabilities, electronic and elastic prop- erties of typical long-period superstructures Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti in Al-rich TiAl alloys together with c-TiAl. The obtained lattice parameters by relaxation of crystalline cells are in good agreement with the experimental data. The calculated formation enthalpies show that r-Al2Ti has the highest structure sta- bility from energetic point of view, and then followed by h-Al2Ti, Al5Ti3 and c-TiAl. The electronic density of states and charge density distribution indicate that due to strong hybridization between Al-2p and Ti-3d, there is a strong directional bonding between Ti and Al atoms. The elastic constants are calculated, suggesting that these structures are mechanically stable. Bulk modulus B, shear modulus G, Young’s mod- ulus E and Poison’s ratio m of polycrystalline materials are derived from the elastic constants. By several criteria, elastic anisotropies are analyzed, showing that these structures possess different degree of anisotropies.

2010 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

h-Al2Ti was observed for the ﬁrst time by Miida et al. [17] and then discussed in many papers [3,5–10,12–14,16,18,19]. r-Al2Ti is well known to be stable phase according to a recent Al–Ti phase dia- gram reported by Schuster and Plam [20]. As the LPSs strongly inﬂuence the plastic deformation behavior of TiAl crystals [5,11,14], the microstructures and phase stabilities of these three LPSs have been studied extensively. Nevertheless, the crystal struc- tures and microstructures of the LPSs are very sensitive to the alloy composition and heat-treatment conditions [3,5–7,10,12,14,18,19], the thermal stabilities and phase transition of these LPSs need to be understood completely and precisely in theory.

Theoretical studies concerning Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti phases are relatively scarce. Only full-potential linearized augmented Sla- ter-type orbital (FLASTO) was carried out for r-Al2Ti previously [23]. Recently, ﬁrst-principles calculation of structural energetics of these three LPSs was carried out by Ghosh and Asta [24]. To the best of our knowledge, there is no theoretical investigation on the mechanical properties for Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti. As structural alloys, the mechanical properties are the basic parame- ters for the technical applications. So it is necessary to gain more fundamental theoretical understanding of these three LPSs.

In present work, ﬁrst-principles calculations have been per- formed for a systematic investigation of the structural stabilities, electronic and elastic properties of Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti in comparison with c-TiAl. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In the next section the computational method em- ployed in the present investigation is described brieﬂy. In Section

3 the structural stabilities, electronic structures and elastic proper- ties of c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti are presented and dis- cussed. Conclusions are summarized in Section 4.

\begin{title}
2. Method
\end{title}

The calculations presented here were performed using the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) [25,26] based on den- sity functional theory (DFT) [27]. The exchange–correlation energy functional was described by the well-established Perdew–Wang (PW91) version of the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) [28], and the ion–electron interactions were treated by the projec- tor augmented wave (PAW) method [29] with 3s, 3p valence states for Al and 3d, 4s valence states for Ti. Wave functions were ex- panded by the plane waves up to energy cutoff of 330 eV for c-TiAl and three LPSs (Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti). Brillouin-zone integra- tions were performed using k-point sampling of Monkhorst–Pack scheme [30]. For optimization of geometrical structure and calcu- lation of elastic constants, 14 14 14, 6 6 14, 14 6 14 and 14 14 4 grids were used for c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r- Al2Ti, respectively. Whereas during calculation of the density of states (DOS) the k-point grids were 16 16 16, 8 8 16, 16 8 16 and 16 16 6, respectively. The ﬁrst order Methfes- sel and Paxton [31] method with a temperature broadening param- eter of 0.2 eV was used for structural relaxation, and the optimization of the atomic structure and the lattice constants was performed for each structure until the residual force and stress in the equilibrium geometry are of the order of 0.01 eV/Å and 10 3 GPa, respectively. The calculations of electronic total energy and DOS were performed using the tetrahedron method with the Blöchl corrections [32]. The convergence test showed that with

\begin{title}
3. Results and discussion
\end{title}

\begin{title}
3.1. Structural stabilities
\end{title}

Fig. 1 shows the superstructures of three typical LPSs Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti together with the structure of c-TiAl. They have different long-periodic stacking sequences based on a face-cen- tered tetragonal lattice. c-TiAl, Al5Ti3 and r-Al2Ti belong to tetrag- onal crystal structures, while h-Al2Ti has an orthorhombic crystal structure. These crystal structures were optimized with relaxation of cell shape and atomic positions. The calculated total energy as a function of volume were ﬁtted to the Birch–Murnaghan equation of state (EOS) [33] to determine cell parameters, equilibrium vol- ume V0 and bulk modulus B0. The obtained results are given in Table 1, together with available experimental and other theoretical data. Clearly, the calculated lattice parameters of c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti are all in good agreement with experimental data. Furthermore, the calculated bulk modulus B0 for c-TiAl is also in good agreement with experimental data. Although experimental measurement of bulk modulus B0 for Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti are not available so far, the calculated results are in good accordance with other theoretical investigations [24].

\begin{title}
3.2. Electronic structures
\end{title}

It is well known that the structure and property of material are closely associated with its electronic states. In order to gain insight into electronic characteristic, the total and partial density of states (DOS) of c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti were calcu- lated and shown in Fig. 2, where the Fermi energy (EF) is set at zero and marked by the vertical lines. For c-TiAl, in the lower en- ergy range from 9.0 eV to 4.0 eV the total DOS is dominantly contributed by 2s states of Al, in the intermediate energy range from 4.0 eV to 0.8 eV the total DOS is dominantly contributed by 2p states of Al and 3d states of Ti, and in the upper energy range from 0.8 eV to 2.6 eV the total DOS is dominantly contrib- uted by 3d states of Ti. The total DOSs of Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti also consist of three different energy ranges and exhibit similar feature. For Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti, the lower energy ranges are from 9.8 eV to 3.7 eV, 9.9 eV to 4.0 eV and 10.0 eV to 4.2 eV, respectively. The intermediate energy ranges expanded up to 0.1 eV, 0.1 eV and 0.0 eV, respectively. The upper limits of the upper energy ranges stretched to 1.6 eV, 1.7 eV and 1.6 eV, respectively. In each energy range the contribution of va- lence electron to the total DOS for Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti are very similar with those of c-TiAl. It suggests that strong hybrid- ization between Al-2p and Ti-3d occur for all of these four struc- tures. Moreover, there are pseudo-gaps around the Fermi energy in the total DOS for all of these four structures. The pseudo-gap also shows the occurrence of the hybridization in these struc- tures. For c-TiAl and h-Al2Ti the Fermi energy falls in the descending part of the DOS peak, whereas for Al5Ti3 and r-Al2Ti the Fermi energies are situated directly in the pseudo-gap. It gen- erally believed that a reduction in DOS at the Fermi level contrib- utes to the stability of a given structure [49]. The value of the total DOS at the Fermi level for c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti is 0.884, 0.688, 0.357 and 0.335 states/eV per atom, respectively. Therefore, r-Al2Ti has the highest structural stability, then fol- lowed by h-Al2Ti, Al5Ti3 and c-TiAl. This is consistent with the above analysis of formation enthalpy.

\begin{title}
4. Conclusions
\end{title}

Based on density function theory, the structural stabilities, electronic structures and elastic properties of typical LPSs Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti along with c-TiAl are investigated. The calcu- lated lattice parameters and bulk modulus obtained by ﬁtting to a Birch–Murnaghan EOS are in good agreement with experimental

and other theoretical results. Calculated formation enthalpies indicate that r-Al2Ti possesses the highest structural stability from the energetic point of view, and then followed by h-Al2Ti, Al5Ti3 and c-TiAl. The DOS shows that the strong hybridization between Al-2p and Ti-3d occur for all of these four structures. The charge density distribution indicates there is a strong directional bonding between the Ti and Al atoms. The obtained single-crystal elastic constants are generally in good agreement with the experimental data and other theoretical values. Meanwhile, the present results suggest that all of these four structures are mechanically stable. Furthermore, the polycrystalline elastic modulus such as bulk modulus B, shear modulus G, Young’s modulus E and Poison’s ratio m are also calculated. At last, the elastic anisotropies of these

Keywords: LPSs First-principles calculations Structural stabilities Electronic structures Elastic properties

As potential candidates for high temperature applications, Ti–Al based intermetallic compounds have been under extensive exper- imental and theoretical studies. These Ti–Al intermetallics have promising properties including excellent elevated-temperature strength, resistance to oxidation and corrosion, relatively low den- sity and high melting point. Compared to Ti-rich alloys, Al-rich TiAl alloys have lower densities and better oxidation resistance due to the formation of protective alumina scales in place of Titanium oxi- des [1]. Therefore, study on Al-rich TiAl alloys has been attractive and needs to be carried out very deeply.

Several Al-rich phases with various long-period superstructures (LPSs) such as Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti, r-Al2Ti, h-Al11Ti5, h-Al5Ti2 and Al3Ti have been observed in the Ti–Al system [2–22]. Among these LPSs, Al5Ti3 (Ga5Ti3-type), h-Al2Ti (Ga2Zr-type) and r-Al2Ti (Ga2Hf-type) are justly on the Al-rich side next to the c-TiAl single-phase. Al5Ti3 was ﬁrst observed in Ti-63 at.% Al annealed at 700 C by Miida et al. [2]. Subsequently, it has frequently been conﬁrmed by various more recent electron microscopy studies on rapidly quenched con- ventionally cast, and/or low temperature annealed (below about 800 C) TiAl alloys in this composition range [3–16]. Metastable

First-principles calculations are performed to study the structural stabilities, electronic and elastic prop- erties of typical long-period superstructures Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti in Al-rich TiAl alloys together with c-TiAl. The obtained lattice parameters by relaxation of crystalline cells are in good agreement with the experimental data. The calculated formation enthalpies show that r-Al2Ti has the highest structure sta- bility from energetic point of view, and then followed by h-Al2Ti, Al5Ti3 and c-TiAl. The electronic density of states and charge density distribution indicate that due to strong hybridization between Al-2p and Ti-3d, there is a strong directional bonding between Ti and Al atoms. The elastic constants are calculated, suggesting that these structures are mechanically stable. Bulk modulus B, shear modulus G, Young’s mod- ulus E and Poison’s ratio m of polycrystalline materials are derived from the elastic constants. By several criteria, elastic anisotropies are analyzed, showing that these structures possess different degree of anisotropies.

h-Al2Ti was observed for the ﬁrst time by Miida et al. [17] and then discussed in many papers [3,5–10,12–14,16,18,19]. r-Al2Ti is well known to be stable phase according to a recent Al–Ti phase dia- gram reported by Schuster and Plam [20]. As the LPSs strongly inﬂuence the plastic deformation behavior of TiAl crystals [5,11,14], the microstructures and phase stabilities of these three LPSs have been studied extensively. Nevertheless, the crystal struc- tures and microstructures of the LPSs are very sensitive to the alloy composition and heat-treatment conditions [3,5–7,10,12,14,18,19], the thermal stabilities and phase transition of these LPSs need to be understood completely and precisely in theory.

Theoretical studies concerning Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti phases are relatively scarce. Only full-potential linearized augmented Sla- ter-type orbital (FLASTO) was carried out for r-Al2Ti previously [23]. Recently, ﬁrst-principles calculation of structural energetics of these three LPSs was carried out by Ghosh and Asta [24]. To the best of our knowledge, there is no theoretical investigation on the mechanical properties for Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti. As structural alloys, the mechanical properties are the basic parame- ters for the technical applications. So it is necessary to gain more fundamental theoretical understanding of these three LPSs.

In present work, ﬁrst-principles calculations have been per- formed for a systematic investigation of the structural stabilities, electronic and elastic properties of Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti in comparison with c-TiAl. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In the next section the computational method em- ployed in the present investigation is described brieﬂy. In Section
3 the structural stabilities, electronic structures and elastic proper- ties of c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti are presented and dis- cussed. Conclusions are summarized in Section 4.

The calculations presented here were performed using the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) [25,26] based on den- sity functional theory (DFT) [27]. The exchange–correlation energy functional was described by the well-established Perdew–Wang (PW91) version of the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) [28], and the ion–electron interactions were treated by the projec- tor augmented wave (PAW) method [29] with 3s, 3p valence states for Al and 3d, 4s valence states for Ti. Wave functions were ex- panded by the plane waves up to energy cutoff of 330 eV for c-TiAl and three LPSs (Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti). Brillouin-zone integra- tions were performed using k-point sampling of Monkhorst–Pack scheme [30]. For optimization of geometrical structure and calcu- lation of elastic constants, 14 14 14, 6 6 14, 14 6 14 and 14 14 4 grids were used for c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r- Al2Ti, respectively. Whereas during calculation of the density of states (DOS) the k-point grids were 16 16 16, 8 8 16, 16 8 16 and 16 16 6, respectively. The ﬁrst order Methfes- sel and Paxton [31] method with a temperature broadening param- eter of 0.2 eV was used for structural relaxation, and the optimization of the atomic structure and the lattice constants was performed for each structure until the residual force and stress in the equilibrium geometry are of the order of 0.01 eV/Å and 10 3 GPa, respectively. The calculations of electronic total energy and DOS were performed using the tetrahedron method with the Blöchl corrections [32]. The convergence test showed that with
the above calculation parameters the error for the total energy is less than 1 meV/atom.

Fig. 1 shows the superstructures of three typical LPSs Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti together with the structure of c-TiAl. They have different long-periodic stacking sequences based on a face-cen- tered tetragonal lattice. c-TiAl, Al5Ti3 and r-Al2Ti belong to tetrag- onal crystal structures, while h-Al2Ti has an orthorhombic crystal structure. These crystal structures were optimized with relaxation of cell shape and atomic positions. The calculated total energy as a function of volume were ﬁtted to the Birch–Murnaghan equation of state (EOS) [33] to determine cell parameters, equilibrium vol- ume V0 and bulk modulus B0. The obtained results are given in Table 1, together with available experimental and other theoretical data. Clearly, the calculated lattice parameters of c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti are all in good agreement with experimental data. Furthermore, the calculated bulk modulus B0 for c-TiAl is also in good agreement with experimental data. Although experimental measurement of bulk modulus B0 for Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti are not available so far, the calculated results are in good accordance with other theoretical investigations [24].

To evaluate the competition among different phases, detailed and accurate information of the structural stabilities is required. Generally, the formation enthalpy DH is a quantity of fundamental interest, which is deﬁned as:

where EAlmTin tot is the total energy of AlmTin, and EAl solid, ETi solid are the to- tal energies per atom of Al with fcc structure and Ti with hcp struc- ture. NAl and NTi refer to the numbers of Al and Ti atoms in unit cell. The calculated results are listed in Table 2, along with available experimental and other theoretical data. As shown in Table 2, the calculated formation enthalpies of these four structures are all

negative, indicating that these structures can exist stably. r-Al2Ti has the lowest formation enthalpy, so it has the highest structural stability from energetic point of view, and then followed by h-Al2Ti, Al5Ti3 and c-TiAl. The present results are also in good agreement with the general experimental measurement and other theoretical calculations [23,24,35,40–42,45–48].

It is well known that the structure and property of material are closely associated with its electronic states. In order to gain insight into electronic characteristic, the total and partial density of states (DOS) of c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti were calcu- lated and shown in Fig. 2, where the Fermi energy (EF) is set at zero and marked by the vertical lines. For c-TiAl, in the lower en- ergy range from 9.0 eV to 4.0 eV the total DOS is dominantly contributed by 2s states of Al, in the intermediate energy range from 4.0 eV to 0.8 eV the total DOS is dominantly contributed by 2p states of Al and 3d states of Ti, and in the upper energy range from 0.8 eV to 2.6 eV the total DOS is dominantly contrib- uted by 3d states of Ti. The total DOSs of Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti also consist of three different energy ranges and exhibit similar feature. For Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti, the lower energy ranges are from 9.8 eV to 3.7 eV, 9.9 eV to 4.0 eV and 10.0 eV to 4.2 eV, respectively. The intermediate energy ranges expanded up to 0.1 eV, 0.1 eV and 0.0 eV, respectively. The upper limits of the upper energy ranges stretched to 1.6 eV, 1.7 eV and 1.6 eV, respectively. In each energy range the contribution of va- lence electron to the total DOS for Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti are very similar with those of c-TiAl. It suggests that strong hybrid- ization between Al-2p and Ti-3d occur for all of these four struc- tures. Moreover, there are pseudo-gaps around the Fermi energy in the total DOS for all of these four structures. The pseudo-gap also shows the occurrence of the hybridization in these struc- tures. For c-TiAl and h-Al2Ti the Fermi energy falls in the descending part of the DOS peak, whereas for Al5Ti3 and r-Al2Ti the Fermi energies are situated directly in the pseudo-gap. It gen- erally believed that a reduction in DOS at the Fermi level contrib- utes to the stability of a given structure [49]. The value of the total DOS at the Fermi level for c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti is 0.884, 0.688, 0.357 and 0.335 states/eV per atom, respectively. Therefore, r-Al2Ti has the highest structural stability, then fol- lowed by h-Al2Ti, Al5Ti3 and c-TiAl. This is consistent with the above analysis of formation enthalpy.
In order to further reveal the feature of bonding, the contour plots of charge density distribution are also investigated. As a representative, Fig. 3 shows the contour plots of charge density

distribution of c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti in the (0 0 1) plane. For c-TiAl, the charge distribution of Ti site is shown to be highly non-spherical. The directional bonding within the (0 0 1) Ti rich layer is may caused by the Al atoms in the (0 0 2) Al layer, and results in an anisotropy charge distribution in the (0 0 1) plane [50]. This suggests that a strong chemical interaction exists between Ti and Al atoms, and this feature is consistent with the DOS plots (Fig. 2a) which shows strong hybridization be- tween Al-2p and Ti-3d. As to Al5Ti3 and h-Al2Ti, the charge distri- bution of Ti site is still shown to be highly non-spherical, and the charge distribution about the Al site is also deformed. It is obvi- ous that strong directional bonding exists between the Ti and

Al atoms, and the directional bonding between Ti atoms is ob- served as well. For r-Al2Ti, the deformation of the charge distribu- tion about the Ti site is much less than those of c-TiAl, Al5Ti3 and h-Al2Ti, and the charge distribution about the Al site is almost spherical.

The calculated elastic constants for single crystal c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti are listed in Table 4. Up to now, the experi- mental and other theoretical investigations of elastic constants are only available for c-TiAl. As shown in Table 4, our calculated elastic constants for c-TiAl are generally in good agreement with the experimental data and other theoretical values. The present calculations showed that the value of C11 (and/or C22) for Al5Ti3 is the largest among these four structures, C11 (and/or C22) for h-Al2Ti is very close to that for r-Al2Ti, whereas c-TiAl has the smallest value. It shows that when compressing along the a (and/or b) axis, c-TiAl is the easiest, while Al5Ti3 is the most dif- ﬁcult. From Table 4, it can be seen that the value of C33 become eventually large from c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti to r-Al2Ti. The varia- tion tendency of C66 for these structures is similar to that of C33, whereas the variation of C44 (and/or C55) exhibit opposite ten- dency. It is noteworthy that c-TiAl has the largest C12, C13 and C23, then followed by r-Al2Ti, Al5Ti3 and h-Al2Ti for C12, by h-Al2Ti, Al5Ti3 and r-Al2Ti for C13, and by Al5Ti3, r-Al2Ti and h-Al2Ti for C23, respectively. Interestingly, C66 is smaller than C44 (and/or C55) for these structures except r-Al2Ti, which means that h-Al2Ti, Al5Ti3 and c-AlTi are more easily deformed by a pure shear along the [0 0 1] axis in comparison with the [1 0 0] (and/or [0 1 0]) axis.

Hence, the elastic properties for polycrystalline aggregates of c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti are also investigated. The theoretical lower and upper bounds to the true polycrystalline bulk modulus B and shear modulus G are given by Reuss (assuming uniform stress throughout a polycrystal) and Voigt (assuming uniform strain). The calculated results of polycrystalline aggregates for c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti are presented in Table 5, which shows good agreement between calculated results and available experi- mental data. The bulk moduli of these four structures are in agree- ment with that obtained through the ﬁt to a Birch–Murnaghan EOS (B0). In general, the large value of shear modulus is an indication of the more pronounced directional bonding between atoms. The va- lue of shear modulus for h-Al2Ti is the largest, and then followed by r-Al2Ti, Al5Ti3 and c-TiAl. As indicated above, there is a strong

directional bonding between Ti and Al atoms, so the larger numbers of Ti–Al bonding for h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti result in larger values of shear modulus, and the smaller number of Ti–Al bonding for c-TiAl also associates with the smaller shear modulus. Moreover, the cal- culated shear modules for these four structures are larger than that of most intermetallic compounds. Young’s modulus is used to pro- vide a measure of the stiffness of the solid, i.e. the larger the value of E, the stiffer the material. From the calculated values, Al5Ti3 and r-Al2Ti are of similar stiffness and are slightly stiffer than h-Al2Ti, whereas h-Al2Ti is much stiffer than c-TiAl. The Poisson’s ratio is also calculated because it measures the stability of a crystal against shear, and the small values of Poisson’s ratio for these four materials indicate that c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, r-Al2Ti and h-Al2Ti exhibit relatively lower stability in descending rank under shearing. Considering the fact that the bulk modulus represents the resistance to fracture, while the shear modulus represents the resistance to plastic defor- mation, Pugh [56] proposed brittleness/ductility criteria using the ratio of bulk to shear modulus of polycrystalline phases (B/G). A high B/G value indicates a tendency for ductility, while a low value indicates a tendency for brittleness. The critical value that separates ductile and brittle materials is about 1.75. The calculated values of B/G for c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti are 1.68, 1.41, 1.25 and 1.16, respectively, suggesting that all of these four structures are apparently prone to brittleness in an ascending order.

It is well known that elastic anisotropy usually induces micro- cracks in materials. Therefore, it is important to calculate elastic anisotropy in structural intermetallics. To quantify the anisotropy of elastic properties in c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti, several different criteria were employed in present work. The shear aniso- tropic factor provides a measure of the degree of anisotropy in the bonding between atoms in different planes. The shear anisotropic factor for the {1 0 0} ({0 1 0}, {0 0 1}) shear planes between the h0 1 1i and h0 1 0i (h1 0 1i and h0 0 1i, h1 1 0i and h0 1 0i, respec- tively) directions are:

For an isotropic crystal the factors A1, A2 and A3 must be one, while any value smaller or greater than one is a measure of the degree of elastic anisotropy. The calculated shear anisotropic factors are sum- marized in Table 6. Consistent with the above discussion of elastic constants, c-TiAl, Al5Ti3 and h-Al2Ti have higher degree of shear anisotropy on the (1 0 0) (and/or (0 1 0)) plane than on the (0 0 1) plane, whereas the shear anisotropy on the (0 0 1) plane of r-Al2Ti is larger than on the (1 0 0) (and/or (0 1 0)) plane. The present cal- culations show c-TiAl has a higher degree of anisotropy than other structures, especially on the (1 0 0) and (0 1 0) planes. This implies that the anisotropy of charge distribution in these planes is high for

c-TiAl, and this is also in accordance with the above contour plots of charge density distribution which shows obvious non-spherical charge distribution in Fig. 3a. For h-Al2Ti, the anisotropy on the (1 0 0) and (0 0 1) planes is slightly larger than that of Al5Ti3, whereas the anisotropy of h-Al2Ti on the (0 1 0) plane is smaller than that of Al5Ti3. r-Al2Ti has the lowest degree of anisotropy on the (1 0 0) and (0 1 0) planes, whereas its anisotropy on the (0 0 1) plane is much larger than that of h-Al2Ti and Al5Ti3.

In addition to shear anisotropy, it is also necessary to consider the anisotropy in linear bulk modulus for an orthorhombic (or tetragonal) crystal. The linear bulk modulus in an arbitrary direc- tion can be calculated from the elastic compliances as [57]:

where l1, l2 and l3 are direction cosines. For an isotropic crystal the three linear bulk modulus must be equal. Our calculated results are given in Table 6, it can be seen that the linear bulk modulus of c-TiAl along the c axis is the largest, so the c axis is the most uncom- pressible for c-TiAl. The smallest linear bulk modulus of Al5Ti3 and h-Al2Ti are along the c and b axes respectively, which associates with the largest compressibility. For r-Al2Ti these three linear bulk modulus almost be equal, so r-Al2Ti has a lower degree of anisot- ropy than other structures.

The elastic anisotropy of a crystal can also be measured by the percentage anisotropy in compressibility and shear: AB = (BV BR)/ (BV + BR) and AG = (GV GR)/(GV + GR) [58]. A value of zero is associ- ated to isotropic elastic constants, while a value of unit (100%) is associated with the largest anisotropy. The percentage of bulk and shear anisotropies are listed in Table 6. All of these four struc- tures exhibit relatively high degree of anisotropy in shear but small anisotropy in compressibility.

Furthermore, the Young’s modulus along different directions is also included to describe the elastic anisotropy. The direction dependent Young’s modulus for orthorhombic (or tetragonal) crys- tal can be deﬁned as [57]:

Fig. 4 illustrates the directional dependence of Young’s modulus of c-TiAl, Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti. For an isotropic system, the Young’s modulus along different directions should exhibit a spher- ical shape. Fig. 4 shows different degrees of deviation from a sphere for these four structures, thus indicating different degrees of anisotropies in Young’s modulus. The deviation is largest for c-TiAl, relatively smaller deviations are for Al5Ti3 and h-Al2Ti, and r-Al2Ti has the smallest deviation. This means the degree of anisotropy in Young’s modulus is highest for c-TiAl, and relatively lower degrees of anisotropy are for Al5Ti3 and h-Al2Ti, while r-Al2Ti has the lowest degree of anisotropy. The anisotropy in Young’s modulus can also be understood by the nature of chemical bonding between atoms. As discussed above, the charge distribu- tion is highly non-spherical for c-TiAl, which associates with high

degree of anisotropy in Young’s modulus. For r-Al2Ti, the deforma- tion of the charge distribution is much less than those of c-TiAl, Al5Ti3 and h-Al2Ti, so r-Al2Ti has the lowest degree of anisotropy in Young’s modulus.

Based on density function theory, the structural stabilities, electronic structures and elastic properties of typical LPSs Al5Ti3, h-Al2Ti and r-Al2Ti along with c-TiAl are investigated. The calcu- lated lattice parameters and bulk modulus obtained by ﬁtting to a Birch–Murnaghan EOS are in good agreement with experimental

and other theoretical results. Calculated formation enthalpies indicate that r-Al2Ti possesses the highest structural stability from the energetic point of view, and then followed by h-Al2Ti, Al5Ti3 and c-TiAl. The DOS shows that the strong hybridization between Al-2p and Ti-3d occur for all of these four structures. The charge density distribution indicates there is a strong directional bonding between the Ti and Al atoms. The obtained single-crystal elastic constants are generally in good agreement with the experimental data and other theoretical values. Meanwhile, the present results suggest that all of these four structures are mechanically stable. Furthermore, the polycrystalline elastic modulus such as bulk modulus B, shear modulus G, Young’s modulus E and Poison’s ratio m are also calculated. At last, the elastic anisotropies of these

structures are discussed by several criteria including the shear anisotropic factor, the linear bulk modulus, the percentage of bulk and shear anisotropies and the direction dependent Young’s modulus.
